parts.title: Test that every feature works
parts.intro: Run these on the real site with a fresh account, the way a new customer would. A feature that works on a developer's laptop with three years of their own data in it is not the same as a feature that works.

sections.title: Getting into Scout
sections.blurb: If someone cannot sign up, nothing else on this page matters.

items.title: Sign up fresh
items.good: The verification code arrives within a minute or so, it is six digits, and the app accepts it.
steps: Open a private or incognito window and go to /app; you land on the Scout sign-in screen.
Click Create an account at the bottom of the card.
Fill First name, Last name, Email (an address never used on Scout), and Password (6 characters minimum), then press Create account.
The screen switches to Check your email. Watch that inbox: a 6-digit code should arrive within a minute or so.
Type it into the Verification code field and press Verify & continue. You should land inside the app.
If nothing arrives, press Resend code once. No email at all is a Broken, not a needs-work.
items.tech: Codes are generated by Supabase and sent through Resend over custom SMTP. The code input accepts exactly six characters, so an eight-digit code setting makes signup impossible.

items.title: Sign up with a taken email
items.good: You are taken to the sign-in screen with a clear message, rather than left waiting on a verify screen for an email that will never arrive.
steps: If you are signed in, log out first: click your email at the bottom of the sidebar, then Log out.
On the sign-in screen, click Create an account.
Fill the form using an email that already has a Scout account and press Create account.
Correct: you are flipped back to the Sign in form with the message: That email already has an account. Try signing in, or reset your password.
Wrong: you are left on the Check your email screen waiting for a code that will never come.
items.tech: Supabase deliberately sends nothing on a repeat signup to avoid leaking which addresses are registered. The app has to detect this and redirect.

items.title: Reset a forgotten password
items.good: A reset code arrives, the new password is accepted, and you can sign in with it straight away.
steps: On the sign-in screen, click Forgot password? (to the right of the Remember me checkbox).
Enter the account's email and press Send reset code.
Get the 6-digit code from the email, then fill Reset code, New password, and Confirm new password, and press Update password.
You should see: Your password is updated. Taking you in.
Prove it stuck: log out (sidebar, click your email, then Log out) and sign back in with the new password.

items.title: Sign in on a second device
items.good: Your profile, projects, and saved work all appear. Nothing has to be re-entered.
steps: On a laptop, set the account up: fill the Profile tab and run one search so Finds has rows.
On a phone, go to /app and sign in with the same email and password.
Open the Profile tab: name, bio or resume text, and LinkedIn should all be filled already.
Open the Finds tab: the same finds with the same statuses.
On the Scout tab, open the project picker in the Scouting for row: the same projects and categories. Nothing should need re-entering.
items.tech: This is the failure the profile-saving migration exists to fix. If it is missing, saves fail silently and everything looks fine until you sign in elsewhere.

tour.text: Checking the second device. Start in Profile: everything you typed on the first device should already be here.
Now Finds: the same finds, with the same status counts along the top.
Finally the Scout tab: the project and category pickers in the Scouting for row should list the same projects. If nothing needed re-entering, mark it Works.

items.title: Stay signed in holds
items.good: Ticking remember me keeps you signed in after closing the browser. Leaving it unticked does not.
steps: Sign in with the Remember me checkbox on the Sign in form ticked. Quit the browser completely (Cmd+Q, not just the tab), reopen it, and return to /app: you should still be inside.
Log out (sidebar, click your email, then Log out), sign in again with Remember me unticked, quit the browser completely, and reopen: this time you should be back on the sign-in screen.

items.title: Switch saved accounts
items.good: You can flip between accounts without re-typing a password, and you never see the other account's data.
steps: In the sidebar, click your email at the very bottom (its tooltip says Switch account). A menu opens.
Press + Add another account and sign in with a second account.
Open the menu again and click the first account's email: you should be switched back without typing a password.
After each switch, check Finds, the project picker on the Scout tab, and Profile: everything should belong to the active account, with no bleed-through from the other one.

tour.text: Your accounts live here: click your email to open the switcher. + Add another account signs a second one in; clicking a listed email hops straight to it, no password. Do the switch yourself.
After switching, look at Finds: the list and the counts must be the other account's, never a mix.

items.title: Sign out fully
items.good: After signing out, pressing back does not show the previous account's data.
steps: In the sidebar, click your email at the bottom, then press Log out.
Press the browser back button several times.
You should only ever see the sign-in screen, never a cached copy of the app still showing the account's data.

tour.text: Log out lives here: click your email, then Log out. Do that yourself, then hammer the back button; you must never see the app's data again, only the sign-in screen.

items.title: Continue-as works next day
items.good: Sign in, spend time in the app AND the admin pages, come back the next day signed out: 'Continue as' signs you straight in, no 'saved session expired' loop. If it does fail once, the error names the reason and your email is prefilled so recovery is one password.
steps: Day one: sign in with Remember me ticked, use the app normally, and also spend time in the /admin pages.
Day two: open /app. If you are signed out, the sign-in screen should show a Continue as button with your name at the top of the card.
Press Continue as. Correct: it flips to Signing in and takes you straight into the app, no password, no saved session expired loop.
If it does fail once, the error must name the reason and the Sign in form below must have your email prefilled, so recovery is one password.

items.title: Bad boot never wipes the profile
items.good: If the profile/state load times out or fails, Scout lets you in but HOLDS all server writes for that session, an all-blank profile can never overwrite a filled row (server-side guard too), and blank server fields never shadow real local ones on merge. Kaitlyn's profile was wiped this way on 2026-08-24 and restored.
steps: Use a TEST account (not your real one). Fill its profile in (name, role, some experience), reload once, and confirm it all comes back. That filled state is your baseline.
Simulate the bad boot: open DevTools (Cmd+Option+I) > Network tab > set throttling to Offline, then reload /app. After ~8 seconds Scout should let you in anyway instead of hanging.
While still in that session, open Profile and poke around; then set throttling back to No throttling and reload normally.
The profile must show EVERYTHING from the baseline. Any field missing = Broken (this is the 2026-08-24 wipe).

The nastier variant: DevTools > Application > Storage > Clear site data, THEN go Offline and reload, so the session boots truly blank. Go back online, sign in, reload: the server copy must still be the full baseline. A blank session must never have pushed its blanks up.

sections.title: Setting up for the first time
sections.blurb: The first ten minutes decide whether someone comes back. Test this with a genuinely empty account.

items.title: Empty account looks welcoming
items.good: Empty screens explain what goes there and what to do next. No zeroes with no context, no blank panels, no error messages.
steps: Sign up fresh, finish setup, then walk the sidebar top to bottom: Dashboard, Scout, Finds, Drafts, Sent, Manual, Applications, Projects, Templates, Profile, Settings.
On each tab ask: does the empty state explain what will live here and what to do next?
Note any bare zero with no context, blank panel, or error-looking message; those are bugs, not invitations.

tour.text: A brand-new account should look inviting everywhere. Start on the Dashboard: the checklist should read as next steps, not as something broken.
Finds, empty: it should say what will land here once you scout, not show a blank table.
Drafts, empty: same test. Then glance at Sent.
Templates: each of the three pages behind this toggle should invite you to add something.
Applications: it should explain that things you apply to gather here. Write down anything that reads as a bug rather than an invitation.

items.title: Onboard a personal account
items.good: The questions make sense, the answers are saved, and what you typed visibly shapes what Scout suggests next.
steps: Sign up fresh. On the Set up your account screen, choose Just me.
Answer everything it asks, being specific about what you do and who you want to reach.
Inside the app, open the Profile tab and confirm every answer is stored in the matching field, word for word.
Type a goal on the Scout tab and check the suggestions visibly lean on what you told it.

tour.text: Your onboarding answers should be sitting here in Profile, exactly as you typed them. Check every field.
And back on the Scout tab, the seeded goal and categories should reflect what you described, not generic filler.

items.title: Onboard a company account
items.good: Same as above, plus the team features appear afterwards.
steps: Sign up a second fresh account. On Set up your account, choose A company, org, or team, then Create a new company.
Try the shortcut first: enter your site under Have a website or social page? Let Scout fill this in and press Read my site; review what it fills.
Complete Company name, What does the company do?, Company stage, and Your role at the company, then press Create company & enter Scout.
Confirm the Team tab now shows in the sidebar.
Open Profile: it should have an About you / Your company toggle, and Your company should hold the details you gave.

tour.text: Company accounts get a Team tab. It should be here in the sidebar now.
And Profile splits in two: flip this toggle to Your company and confirm the company details you entered during setup all carried over.

items.title: Starter projects fit you
items.good: Scout suggests projects and search categories that match what you described, not generic filler like coffee chats.
steps: During onboarding, describe something specific, for example a student org booking speakers for a spring showcase.
On the Scout tab, open the two pickers in the Scouting for row above the goal box: the project, then its categories.
The suggested project and categories should reference speakers and showcases, not generic filler like coffee chats.
items.tech: Generated by the starter plan route from the profile text.

tour.text: The pickers above this goal box hold your starter project and its categories. Open both: they should be about what you described in setup, not a generic template.

items.title: Profile survives overnight
items.good: Fill in the profile, close everything, come back the next day, and it is all still there.
steps: Open the Profile tab and fill it completely: bio or resume text, LinkedIn, and the rest.
Log out (sidebar, click your email at the bottom, then Log out), close the browser, and come back the next day.
Sign in and open Profile: every field must still be filled. Anything re-blanked is a Broken.

tour.text: Fill everything on this tab, then log out via your email at the bottom of the sidebar. Tomorrow, this same tab must still hold all of it with nothing to re-enter.

items.title: Resume upload fills the fields
items.good: It pulls out the name and a likely use case, leaves blank anything it cannot find, and never makes something up.
steps: Open the Profile tab and find the upload area labeled Drop your resume or LinkedIn here, or click to upload.
Drop a real resume PDF on it (an image is rejected with a plain message; that is correct).
Check every field it pre-fills against the document: name, background, likely use case.
Anything it could not find should stay blank. Anything invented is a Broken, not a needs-work.

tour.text: This is the drop zone: give it a real resume PDF and watch which fields fill.
Now audit: every pre-filled field must trace back to the document. Blank is fine; invented is Broken.

items.title: Walkthrough works for a stranger
items.good: A person who did not build this can follow it without asking questions.
steps: Sit someone outside the team in front of it.
Do not help them. Write down every place they hesitate.

items.title: Dictation works everywhere offered
items.good: The mic button appears only in browsers that support it, and dictated text lands in the right field.
steps: In Chrome, on the Scout tab, look at the right edge of the Who are you looking for? box: a Dictate button with a mic icon sits there. Press it, speak, and confirm your words land in the goal box.
The same Dictate button appears on the New project description, the deny reason box, and template text boxes; spot-check one of those too.
Open the same screens in Firefox (no speech support): the button should simply not render. No dead button, no error.

tour.text: The Dictate mic sits at the right edge of this goal box. Press it, talk, and your words should appear in the box. In a browser without speech support this button hides itself entirely.

items.title: Project name retunes categories
items.good: A project named for a different world (say, Grad School) gets starter categories about that world, not leftovers from your last project.
steps: On the Scout tab, open the category picker in the Scouting for row and choose + New project.
Name it something clearly outside your usual work, like Grad School, add a one-line description under What is it looking for?, and press Create and start scouting.
Open the category picker again, or the Projects tab: the starter categories should be about that new world, not leftovers from your last project.
items.tech: New projects used to inherit the previous project's use case, which is why a Grad School project could open with Sync & Licensing.

tour.text: Open the category picker above this goal box and pick + New project. Name it for a different world, like Grad School, describe it in one line, and press Create and start scouting.
Now check Projects: the new project's categories should fit its world, with nothing carried over from your usual work.

items.title: Delete the last project
items.good: Deleting your only project is allowed; Scout drops you into a fresh blank one instead of refusing.
steps: On a test account, open the Projects tab.
Select a project and press Delete in its action row (the confirm dialog names how many categories and finds go with it). Repeat until none are left.
Correct: Scout drops you into a fresh blank project rather than refusing to delete the last one or showing an error.

tour.text: Projects are deleted here: select one and press Delete in its action row. On a TEST account, remove every project, confirming each dialog.
After the last one goes you should land in a clean, untitled project, ready to use. An error or a refusal is the fail.

items.title: Empty runs make no categories
items.good: Running the project-level search, or a goal nearly identical to the project description or an existing category, does not mint a redundant category. A genuinely new goal still saves itself.
steps: On the Scout tab, pick a saved category in the picker and press Scout. When it finishes, open the Projects tab: no near-duplicate of that category should have appeared (fail if one did).
Back on Scout, open the category picker, choose New search, type a clearly different goal, and run it: that one SHOULD save itself as a new category.
The switch lives in Settings under Searching: Save new searches as categories. Turn it off and confirm new goals stop saving themselves.

tour.text: Run a saved category from here first (pressing Scout spends one search, so run it yourself).
In Projects: that run must NOT have minted a duplicate category. A genuinely new goal, run via the picker's New search entry, should appear here.
The off switch is here in Settings, under Searching: Save new searches as categories.

items.title: New search reads as a choice
items.good: The category picker ends with 'New search' for a one-off goal; there is no separate Solo Search pill any more, and nothing near the picker can be mistaken for the run button.
steps: Show the Scout tab to someone new and ask them to start a search.
They should press the big cream Scout button on the first try.

items.title: Dictation shows words live
items.good: Pressing Dictate flips the button to Listening… and your words stream into the field live while you speak, so it never looks dead.
steps: On the Scout tab, press the Dictate mic at the right edge of the Who are you looking for? box.
Speak a full sentence. The button should flip to Listening… and your words should appear in the goal box while you are still talking, not only after you stop.

tour.text: Press the Dictate mic beside this box and speak. Words should stream into the box live, and the button reads Listening… until you stop.

items.title: Add LinkedIn lands right
items.good: The dashboard checklist's Add your LinkedIn button opens Profile AND scrolls to the resume/LinkedIn drop zone, not just the top of the tab.
steps: Click Add your LinkedIn from the dashboard checklist.
You should arrive with the upload area centred on screen.

items.title: Templates splits into three pages
items.good: Outreach, Application materials, and Email signatures are separate pages switched at the top, no scrolling between worlds. Cover letters are written, uploaded, or pasted IN Application materials; the outreach builder is not involved.
steps: Flip through all three pages.
Write and upload a cover letter without leaving Application materials.

tour.text: This is the Templates page toggle: Outreach, Application materials, and Email signatures are three separate pages, no scrolling between worlds.
Click through all three pages. Each should swap in place, and cover letters live under Application materials, not the outreach builder.

items.title: Your links prefill
items.good: The Your links card starts filled with what Scout already knows (LinkedIn, account email, site/phone when present) and stays editable; nothing you typed is ever overwritten. Every kit surfaces them with copy buttons.
steps: On a fresh device, open Application materials and confirm the prefill.
Edit one, reload, confirm your edit stuck.

tour.text: Scout is taking you to Templates. Switch to the Application materials page with this toggle.
Find the Your links card: Website, LinkedIn, Contact email, Phone. The fields should ALREADY hold what Scout knows about you (your LinkedIn from Profile, your account email), without you typing them.
Change one field (say the phone), reload the page, and check the change stuck. Nothing you typed should ever be overwritten by the prefill.
Open any application kit: the same links should appear under Your links with copy buttons. If all that held, mark it Works.

items.title: Templates mint projects
items.good: In Templates' Where-it-applies picker (a house-styled dropdown, not the OS menu), '+ New project…' opens an inline name field; Create makes the project and scopes the template to it in one motion, same as Add-a-contact.
steps: Open the Templates tab, stay on the Outreach page, and start or edit a template.
Scroll to Where it applies and open the project dropdown: it should be the house-styled dropdown, not the bare OS menu.
Choose + New project: an inline name field appears in place. Type a name and press Create.
The project is created and the template is scoped to it in one motion; the dropdown now shows the new project selected, the same move Add-a-contact makes.

tour.text: This is Where it applies. Open the project dropdown: house-styled, not the OS menu.
Pick + New project, name it inline, and press Create. The project should now exist with this template scoped to it, all in one motion.

items.title: Profile splits into two pages
items.good: On a company account, Profile is two pages behind a top toggle: your role and experience on one, the company details and color on the other. No scrolling through the company card to reach your own fields.
steps: On a company account, open the Profile tab.
At the top sits a two-page toggle: About you and Your company.
About you holds your role and experience; Your company holds the company details and the Company color. Confirm neither page makes you scroll through the other's content to reach your own fields.

tour.text: Here is the toggle: About you for your own fields, Your company for the company card and its color. Flip between them; you should never scroll through the company card to reach yourself.

items.title: Personal use checkbox
items.good: With personal use allowed (or as a company owner), a Personal use checkbox appears under the company picker in the sidebar; checking it moves you out of the company lens, your work there stays out of company views, and unchecking returns you. It survives a refresh and does not snap off when you have no personal projects yet.
steps: As a company owner, open Profile, the company page, and turn on Allow personal use. Save.
Check the Personal use checkbox in the sidebar and run a search: the project it creates should not appear to teammates or in the company lens.
Refresh: still checked. Uncheck: back to the company.
On an account whose company has it off (and who owns no company), confirm the checkbox is absent.

sections.title: Finding the right people
sections.blurb: The core promise of the product. If results are thin or made up, nothing downstream matters.

items.title: Scout restates your goal first
items.good: Before spending a search, it reflects back what it thinks you are looking for, and you recognise your own request in it.
steps: On the Scout tab, type a goal into the Who are you looking for? box and press Scout.

Before any searching, Scout runs an Understanding phase (Reading your goal…). It either flashes Scout understands your inquiry, or opens A couple of things before Scout runs with a percent ring and its reading of your request.
Read that back: you should recognize your own request in it.
Re-press Scout later on the unchanged goal: the understanding pass is cached and free; only the run itself spends a search.
items.tech: The understanding pass decomposes the goal only, with no searching and no metering.

tour.text: Type your goal here.

Press Scout yourself (one run spends one search). It starts with an Understanding phase: watch for either the Scout understands your inquiry flash or the questions panel with the percent ring, and check you recognize your request in it.

items.title: Vague goals get a question
items.good: A vague request gets one or two clarifying questions, not a shrug and a bad search.
steps: On the Scout tab, type something deliberately thin, like find me people in music, and press Scout.
Correct: the panel A couple of things before Scout runs opens with one or two multiple-choice questions (chips, plus Any / all and Other…) before anything is searched.
Answer one and press Run Scout with these; the results should reflect your answer. Wrong: it shrugs and runs a bad search with no questions.

tour.text: Type a deliberately vague goal here, like find me people in music.
Press Scout yourself (it spends a search). A vague goal should stop at A couple of things before Scout runs with chip questions; answer one, then Run Scout with these.

items.title: Run all three use cases
items.good: Networking, job and internship hunting, and music PR each return people you would genuinely contact.
steps: On the Scout tab, use the project picker in the Scouting for row to select the matching project for each use case in turn: networking, jobs and internships, and music PR.
For each, type a real goal into the Who are you looking for? box and press Scout.
When each run finishes, open Finds and count how many of the top ten you would genuinely contact.
Under three out of ten for any use case is a needs-work.

tour.text: Pick the use case's project in the picker above, type a real goal here, and press Scout. Repeat for all three worlds: networking, jobs, music PR.
Judge each run here: would you genuinely reach out to at least three of the top ten?

items.title: Odd goals still work
items.good: We promise Scout adapts to any free-text use case, so a request outside the templates has to produce sensible results.
steps: On the Scout tab, open the category picker, choose New search, and type a goal from a completely different world, for example wedding venues in Nashville that host live bands.
Press Scout and let it finish.
Judge the results in Finds exactly as you would a normal run: real, reachable, on-topic.

tour.text: Pick New search in the category picker and type a goal from a totally different world, like wedding venues that host live bands.
Press Scout yourself and judge the results like any other run: sensible, real, reachable.

items.title: Finds are real people
items.good: Names, roles, outlets, and links all check out when you click through.
steps: Open the Finds tab and pick five results at random from a recent run.
Click each row to open its detail view.
Click every link in it: Open site, the source links under the evidence, and any LinkedIn link.
Verify the person actually holds that role at that place today. Any invented person or wrong role is a Broken.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Pick five rows at random and open each one.
In the detail view, click Open site and every source link, and confirm the person, role, and outlet all check out. One fake is a Broken.

items.title: Why-it-fits is true
items.good: The why it fits line refers to something you can confirm on the linked page, not a plausible-sounding guess.
steps: Open five finds and read the Why it fits section in each detail view.
For every specific claim, click through the source links and confirm the claim appears on the actual page.
Flag anything that sounds specific but cannot be traced to a source.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Open a find and read its Why it fits. Every specific claim must be checkable on the linked page, not a plausible-sounding guess.

items.title: Fit scores sort good from bad
items.good: The high scoring results really are better than the low scoring ones. If the order is random, the score is worse than useless.
steps: Open Finds after a run and, ignoring the scores, rank the top ten yourself by how likely you would be to contact each one.
Now compare your order with the fit scores on the cards: the high scorers should broadly be your top picks.
If score order and your judgment look unrelated, the score is worse than useless.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Cover the scores, rank the top ten yourself, then compare with the fit scores on these cards. High should mean better.

items.title: No duplicates or repeats
items.good: The same person does not appear twice in one search, and does not come back in the next search either.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a search, and when it finishes press Scout again with the same goal.
Open Finds and read through both runs' results: nobody should appear twice, within one run or across the two.
Look for near-duplicates too: the same person under two spellings, or with and without an accent.

tour.text: Run a search from here, then run the exact same goal again (each press spends a search).
Now read the list: no one should appear twice, and watch for the same person under two spellings.

items.title: Short names search sensibly
items.good: Typing something like radio DJs or panelists gives Scout enough to find the right people, using your profile for context.
steps: Open the Projects tab, select a project, type a bare name like radio DJs into the New category name box, and press Add category. Add two or three this way.
Pick each new category in the Scout tab's category picker and read the goal Scout wrote for it.
Each goal should be specific and correct, using your profile for context, not your two words echoed back.

tour.text: Add a category by name only: type something like radio DJs into New category name and press Add category.
Now pick that category above this goal box: the goal Scout wrote for it should be specific and correct, grounded in your profile.

items.title: Deep scan adds real info
items.good: It returns facts you did not already have, all traceable to a source.
steps: Open Finds and pick a find whose page you already know well and which has no email or handle yet; the button only shows when there is no contact.
Open its detail view and press Scan for contact (its hint reads: Read this page for a specific contact and any submission requirements).
It shows Scanning…, then reports what it found. Check the new facts are true, new to you, and traceable to the page.
If it finds nothing, the honest message (the site may block bots, try Open site) is correct behavior, not a fail.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Open a find that has no email or handle yet.
This is the button: Scan for contact. Press it, then judge what comes back against the actual page: true, new, traceable.

items.title: Previews load
items.good: The preview shows the actual site, quickly, without breaking the page.
steps: Open the Finds tab and switch to grid view with the Grid view button beside the filters.
Scroll a full page of tiles: each leads with a live preview of the find's site.
Note any preview that hangs, comes back blank, or makes scrolling stutter.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Switch to Grid view with the toggle next to these filters, then scroll a full page: every preview should load fast, none blank, none dragging the page down.

items.title: Over-pitched contacts rest
items.good: Once a handful of different Scout users have reached out to the same person, that person stops appearing for everyone else.
steps: Ask a developer to confirm the cap is switched on and to show it working with test data.
This is the difference between an outreach tool and a spam tool, so it is worth proving rather than assuming.
items.tech: Backed by the shared contact ledger. It only works once the exposure table exists in the production database.

items.title: Denies change the next run
items.good: After you pass on several results for the same reason, the next search shows fewer like them.
steps: In Finds, press Deny on five results that share a problem. Each time the Why? Pick a reason… picker opens, choose the same reason, for example Wrong industry.
Run a similar search from the Scout tab.
The new results should show visibly fewer of that pattern; identical output means nothing was learned.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Deny sits on each find next to Approve. Deny five with the SAME reason from the Why? picker.
Now run a similar search and compare: the denied pattern should be fading.

items.title: A slow search keeps you company
items.good: Long runs show real progress, so the app never looks frozen.
steps: Open DevTools (Cmd+Option+I), go to the Network tab, and set throttling to Slow 3G.
On the Scout tab, run a broad search.
While it runs, something must keep moving: the progress card lines, the found counter, the Time saving numbers. Any stretch where the screen sits frozen with nothing changing is a fail.
Set throttling back to No throttling when done.

tour.text: Throttle your connection with DevTools (Network tab, Slow 3G), then run a broad search from here and watch: the progress card must keep talking the whole time.

items.title: Empty searches explain why
items.good: You are told why and given something to try, not shown an empty box.
steps: On the Scout tab, search for something deliberately impossible, for example left-handed theremin repair shops in Antarctica.
When it comes back empty or nearly empty, read what the results area says.
It should say why and offer something concrete to try, not show a bare empty box. Judge it as a real user would.

tour.text: Type an impossible goal here and run it. The empty outcome must explain itself and suggest a next move, not leave a blank box.

items.title: Previews need sign-in
items.good: Signed in, previews load fast and can be resized with the drag bar under them. Signed out, the preview area shows a polite sign-in page with a direct link to the site.
steps: Signed in, open a find's detail view: the website preview pane should load the real site quickly.
Grab the handle under the preview (Drag to resize the preview) and drag: the pane should resize.
Right-click inside the preview and use the browser's frame menu (in Chrome: Open frame in new tab), then copy that tab's address.
Paste it into a private window: you should get a polite sign-in page with a direct link to the site, never the proxied site itself.
items.tech: The preview used to be an open proxy anyone on the internet could route traffic through; it now needs a short-lived signed pass that only signed-in users get.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Open any find: the preview should already be showing the live site.
This bar resizes the preview: drag it. Then do the private-window check from the steps; the raw preview address must demand sign-in.

items.title: Websites are the real site
items.good: New finds never list a Yelp or YellowPages listing page as the company's site. If no real site is known, the field is empty and the listing stays under evidence.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a search for local companies, for example family-owned coffee roasters in Nashville.
In each find's detail view, click the Website row in the contact column.

It must land on the company's own site. A Yelp, YellowPages, or other directory listing in that field is a fail; when no real site is known the field should be empty, with the listing kept under evidence.

tour.text: Run a local-companies search from here.
Open each find and click its Website row: the company's own site every time, never a review or directory page.

items.title: Hand-adds steer searches
items.good: After you add a few people by hand, the next search in that project leans toward more people like them.
steps: Open the Manual tab and use Add a contact. Add two or three people of one very specific type, pressing Autofill the rest after typing each name.
Back on the Scout tab, run a search in the same project.
Judge whether the results lean toward that type more than before.

tour.text: Scout is opening Add a contact for you. Add two or three people of one very specific type.
Now run a search in the same project and see whether the results lean toward the people you added.

items.title: Index helps without cloning results
items.good: Searches quietly reuse people Scout has already verified, but two accounts running the same goal still get clearly different result sets, and fresh-from-the-web people always make up the majority.
steps: Open two browsers (or one normal + one private window): your account in one, a second account (Suri's, or a fresh signup) in the other.
Run the SAME goal text on both within a few minutes, e.g. 'indie playlist curators who take bedroom pop submissions'.
Put the two Finds lists side by side and compare names: mostly different people with some overlap is correct; near-identical lists is Broken.

Spot-check both lists: most finds should cite a live page (source link opens and mentions them), which is what fresh-from-the-web looks like. Every reused one still needs a true, checkable reason it fits THIS goal.
items.tech: Index candidates are capped at a small minority per search, sampled differently per user, expire from rotation after 90 days, and pass the same fit scoring and exposure caps as fresh candidates.

items.title: People-goals run as networking
items.good: A goal about alumni, mentors, or people open to a chat returns PEOPLE with strong fits, never the 'few active postings matched' banner, even when the project is about applying to programs or jobs.
steps: On the Scout tab, pick a job or grad-school project in the project picker.
Type a people goal like alumni of my program open to a coffee chat and press Scout.
Results must be people with real fit scores. The word outlets, employer cards, or the few active postings matched banner on a people search is a Broken.
items.tech: The goal text overrides the project's use case when it unambiguously asks for people, not openings.

tour.text: With a job project picked above, type a people goal here, like alumni open to a coffee chat, and run it. People with fit scores must come back, never a postings banner.

items.title: People-searches sweep LinkedIn
items.good: An alumni or professionals search returns several results whose contact route is a LinkedIn profile, pulled from LinkedIn's public pages, not just news articles and school spotlights.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a clearly people-shaped search: alumni of a program, or professionals in a niche.
In Finds, count how many results carry a linkedin.com/in profile link as their contact route.
Several should. Zero LinkedIn results on a people search is a needs-work.
items.tech: Dedicated search queries scoped to linkedin.com; public pages only, no login.

tour.text: Run a people-shaped search from here: alumni of a program, professionals in a niche.
Count the results whose contact route is a LinkedIn profile. Zero on a people search is a needs-work.

items.title: Right platforms per goal
items.good: The progress log names the platforms it swept, and they fit the request: alumni searches sweep LinkedIn and university pages, music searches sweep music profiles and Instagram, developer searches sweep GitHub, press searches sweep journalist sites. A wedding-venue search should not be sweeping music sites.
steps: On the Scout tab, run searches in two very different worlds, for example indie playlist curators, then wedding venues.
During each run, read the progress card lines under the stage: they name the platforms being swept.

The platforms must fit the goal: LinkedIn and university pages for alumni, music profiles and Instagram for music, GitHub for developers, journalist sites for press. A music sweep on a non-music search is a needs-work.
items.tech: Up to three platform sweeps per search, chosen from the goal text; public pages only, no logins.

tour.text: Run two searches in very different worlds and watch the progress card each time: the platforms it names must fit the goal.

items.title: Rosters reach the unGoogleable
items.good: A search naming a specific school, employer, or job title returns people the open web would never surface, with real names, roles, companies, and LinkedIn profiles. The progress log says it checked the people directory and how many match.
steps: On the Scout tab, search for alumni of a named school or people with a named job title, for example Belmont music business alumni working in touring.
Watch the progress card for the line saying it checked the people directory and how many match.
The results should include real people, with names, roles, companies, and LinkedIn profiles, beyond the handful with press coverage.
Run a vague goal with no hard filter and confirm the directory is skipped entirely; that is correct, not a bug.
items.tech: Licensed people directory (People Data Labs) queried only when the goal names a school, company, title, or industry; results pass the same fit and exposure gates as web finds.

tour.text: Type a goal that names a school or a job title, run it, and watch the progress card for the people-directory line. The results should include people the open web alone would never surface.

items.title: Home base boosts nearby
items.good: With a base set, results in that region come first, and strong matches elsewhere still appear further down rather than vanishing.
steps: Open Profile, switch to the Your company page, set the company location to a city like Seattle, and save.
On the Scout tab, run a search whose targets are national.
Nearby results should rank near the top, and strong matches elsewhere should still appear further down rather than vanishing.
Add remote or anywhere to the goal text and rerun: the location should stop steering the results.
Clear the location field and confirm searches behave as they did before.
items.tech: The base is passed to the planner as a preference, and the prompt tells it to put the wider region in preferred and weight proximity in ranking_factors, never a hard_constraint. If matches outside the region disappear entirely, the model is treating it as a filter and the wording needs tightening.

tour.text: The company location lives on the Your company page behind this toggle. Set it to a test city first.
Now run a national search: nearby first, elsewhere still present further down, never filtered out.

items.title: No location, no steering
items.good: Results sit wherever the best matches are. No single city or region dominates, and nothing in the plan mentions a place nobody typed.
steps: Use an account with no location in the profile and no company base set.
Run a search whose goal names no place at all, for example people in the sports industry to talk to.
Read where the results are actually based. They should be spread out, not clustered in one metro.
Repeat on a second fresh account to be sure it is not one profile carrying a stale value.
If one region keeps winning, check whether any city is named in the planner prompt itself.
items.tech: This regressed once already: the HOME BASE rule in DECOMPOSE_SYS illustrated widening a region with real place names, and since they were the only cities in the prompt, goals with no location borrowed them as a default. The rule is now written without any place names, and says outright that with no base stated, location stays out of required, preferred, hard_constraints and ranking_factors. Empty location must mean no geography, not a fallback.

items.title: Location narrows as meant
items.good: You have decided, deliberately, how strict a location should be, and what the app does matches that decision.
steps: Set a location: yours on Profile's About you page, or the company's on Your company.
On the Scout tab, run a search whose best matches are mostly elsewhere, and count how many out-of-area results survive.
Include one target in the same state but a different metro, and note how it is treated.
Decide deliberately whether that strictness is what you want; if not, that is a scoring rule to change, not a bug to log.
items.tech: Two stages disagree today. The planner treats a base as a soft preference (wider region in preferred, proximity weighted in ranking_factors). The extract prompt's LOCATION ALIGNMENT clause is far harsher: anything outside the exact metro is pinned to a fit_score of 0.01, and same-state-different-metro counts as a mismatch. So the soft preference described at plan time is overridden at scoring time. Pick one behavior and make both stages say it.

tour.text: Set your location on this tab first (About you, or Your company for a company base).
Then run a search whose best matches sit elsewhere and count what survives. The strictness you see should be the strictness you chose.

items.title: Role searches ask where
items.good: A role-shaped search that never says remote or on-site pauses to ask, with one-tap answers, and the answer visibly changes who comes back.
steps: On the Scout tab, search for a kind of role with no mention of where the work happens, for example social media internships at record labels.
Correct: before running, the questions panel (A couple of things before Scout runs) asks about remote, hybrid, or on-site with one-tap chips.
Answer it, run, and confirm who comes back reflects the answer.
Run a goal that already says remote: it must NOT ask again.
Re-run the first goal: a question you already answered must not be asked twice.
items.tech: The planner caps understanding at 85 for a role-shaped goal with no work arrangement stated, which keeps it under the gate that would otherwise run the search silently. A category that scored 100 on an earlier run used to bury this; the gate now uses the current read whenever there are open questions. Answered questions are banked so they are never re-asked.

tour.text: Type a role goal with no remote or on-site mention and press Scout. It should pause with one-tap chips asking where the work happens; your answer must visibly change who comes back.

items.title: Every find is reachable
items.good: Every find has an email, a phone number, or a handle. Not one is a bio page with no way to get in touch.
steps: Run a few searches across different use cases, including one for a sport, a league, or a club.
Open every find: each must carry a real email, phone number, or handle. A profile or bio page on its own does not count.
On the Scout tab after a run, press See what was filtered (N) and confirm the no-contact drops read no way to contact them.
Try a roster or staff-directory search, the kind where pages list names and nothing else, and confirm those names do not come through.
items.tech: The gate is in discover(), keyed on an actual contact value, contactEmail, contactPhone or contactHandle, never on the channel field, which is only the extractor's guess at a route and gets set to things like "Website Form" on results carrying no contact detail at all. That loophole is how a Reign FC player with only a bio page once got through. The gate runs after the Phase 2 enrichment pass so anyone whose address was about to be found still gets that chance.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Check every find's contact details: an email, phone, or handle, always. A bare bio page in the pipeline breaks the rule.
This button opens what was dropped: the no-contact drops should say so plainly.

items.title: Contact rule isn't starving results
items.good: Searches still come back with a useful number of people. When one is thin, the skipped list explains why rather than leaving it looking broken.
steps: Run the searches you would actually run and note how many finds each returns; compare with what those same searches used to give you.
For a thin run, press See what was filtered (N) on the Scout tab and count how many were dropped for having no contact.
If good people are being lost rather than genuinely unreachable ones, the fix is raising the enrichment budget, not relaxing the rule.
items.tech: Requiring a contact route necessarily returns fewer people, which is the intended trade. The lever is the Phase 2 enrichment pass in discover(): it chases contacts for only six finds per search to stay inside the time budget, prioritizing those with no contact at all since they are the ones facing deletion. Raising that six recovers people without loosening the rule, at the cost of a slower search.

tour.text: After a thin run, open this: See what was filtered. Count the no-contact drops; the list is what keeps a thin run from looking broken.

items.title: Starring floats to top
items.good: The star fills with the color set in the profile, the find jumps to the top of the list, and it is still counted in its status tab rather than disappearing from it.
steps: Open Finds and star something near the bottom of the list.
Confirm it moves straight to the top and the star fills in.
Check the star's color matches the one picked in Profile, then change that color and confirm the star follows.
Confirm the status counts along the top did not drop, starring marks a find, it does not move it out of New or Sent.
Star two or three, and confirm they sit together at the top in the order you starred them.
Reload the page and confirm the stars and the order survive.
Change the sort and confirm starred finds still lead.
items.tech: Starred finds are sorted to the front after the chosen sort is applied, so the sort still orders everything below them. This replaced the old pushpin, which pulled a find OUT of its status list into a separate Pinned tab; the tab remains as a filter for seeing only starred finds. The star's color is set inline from --c-brown, the brand token a chosen accent overrides, it was set via the text-accent class first, which is on the element but loses somewhere in the row's cascade and rendered muted grey.

items.title: Job runs return employers
items.good: On a job or internship search, every result is either a specific posting or a company you could approach. No plain LinkedIn profiles or staff bios of people who merely work somewhere.
steps: On the Scout tab, pick the Work Opportunities project (or any job project) in the project picker and run a job search.
Scan Finds: every result must be either a specific posting or a company you could approach.
A bare LinkedIn profile or staff bio with no opening attached is a fail; a recruiter passes only when named as the contact ON a specific opening.

tour.text: Pick a job project above and run a job search from here.
Scan the results: postings and approachable employers only. A person's profile with no opening attached is a fail.

items.title: Five finds minimum
items.good: A search never comes back with one or two finds. Under five, Scout widens on its own and fills the rest with fittable employers to cold-email, and a banner says plainly that those are not confirmed openings.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a deliberately narrow search where live postings are scarce, for example vinyl mastering internships in Kansas.
Count the finds: five or more, always.
Read the banner over the results: when Scout widened into cold-outreach employers to fill the count, it must say plainly that those are not confirmed openings.

tour.text: Type a deliberately narrow goal here and run it. Five or more must come back, and the banner over the results must be honest about any cold-outreach fallback.

items.title: World-denies hard-filter
items.good: After denying with a reason like 'I don't want to work in country music', later searches never surface results squarely in that world, not even as low-fit.
steps: In Finds, press Deny on a find. In the Why? Pick a reason… picker choose Other reason and type the world you want out, for example I don't want to work in country music.
Run two or three more searches in that category from the Scout tab.
Nothing squarely in that world should come back, not even as a low-fit result.

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Deny one from here, and type the unwanted world under Other reason in the Why? picker.
Run a few more searches in the category: that world must be gone entirely.

items.title: Timing denies get a watch
items.good: Denying with 'no open positions' does not banish the company. It can come back occasionally as a check-in, and comes back prominently when it actually has a live opening, saying positions have opened since you last checked.
steps: In Finds, press Deny on a company and type No open positions under Other reason in the Why? picker.
Run several searches in that category over the following days.
The company must not be banished forever: an occasional return should be labeled as a re-check, and it should come back prominently, saying positions have opened, when it actually has a live opening.

tour.text: Deny a company from here with the typed reason No open positions (use Other reason in the Why? picker). Over the following days it should resurface as a re-check, not vanish forever.

items.title: Criteria answered as fields
items.good: Opening a new find shows static labeled rows answering the goal's explicit asks: Remote? In person, Vancouver. Paid? Not stated. Answers come from the source; silent sources say Not stated, never a guess.
steps: Run a search whose goal states criteria (remote or in person, paid, timeframe).
Open a NEW find (old finds predate this) and check the left rail above Why it fits.
Verify each answer against the actual page.

items.title: Impossible requirements disqualify
items.good: A program that requires an affiliation the profile clearly lacks (a specific school, members only, residency) never shows up as a fit. When you DO meet a stated requirement, Why it fits says so.
steps: Make sure your Profile names your school and location, then run a search for programs or mentorships on the Scout tab.
Open each find's page and look for stated requirements: a specific school, members only, residency.
Any find scored as a fit whose page limits participation to a group your profile is not in is a fail (the UBC mentor program bug). When you DO meet a stated requirement, Why it fits should say so.

tour.text: With your school and location in Profile, run a programs search from here.
Open each find's page and hunt for requirements you cannot meet. One of those scored as a fit is the fail.

items.title: Posting seasons steer advice
items.good: The shared index remembers stated posting windows ('Opens each January') and the months live postings were seen, and searches check an org right as its window opens.
steps: Hard to test directly; spot-check that a find whose page states an application window shows it in the criteria rows.
Over time, watch whether recurring programs (annual internships) resurface at the right time of year.
items.tech: Cadence lives on the people_index rows (postingWindow + postingMonths in the opp JSON) and feeds the query planner's index compass with the current month.

items.title: Public Handshake pages appear
items.good: Job searches sweep joinhandshake.com. Yield is thin by design: Handshake walls most postings behind login and Scout only sees public pages.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a student-flavored job search, for example marketing internships for college students.
In Finds, look for any result linking to joinhandshake.com.
None appearing is acceptable: Handshake walls most postings behind login and Scout only sees public pages. A Handshake login page surfacing as a find is the fail.

tour.text: Run a student-flavored job search from here, then scan the results for joinhandshake.com links. Thin yield is fine; a login page as a find is not.

items.title: Refresh stops a run
items.good: Closing or refreshing the tab aborts the search server-side instead of burning credits in the background.
steps: On the Scout tab, start a search and note the live find counter.
Refresh the page mid-run.
After the reload, watch the Finds tab for a minute: the count must not keep climbing. New finds trickling in after the refresh means the server run was not aborted and is still burning credits.

tour.text: Start a search from here, then refresh mid-run (the walkthrough ends with the refresh). Afterward, watch Finds for a minute: the count must hold still.

items.title: The progress log stays readable
items.good: The live search log spreads side to side, clips long queries, and if the same status line would print again back-to-back it prints once with a count (like 'Skipped a duplicate (x4)') instead of repeating. It never grows past the screen.
steps: Start a search and watch the progress card.
Confirm two columns on a wide screen and no line running off the card.

items.title: Timers are honest
items.good: Under the reading deck: Time saving leads at display size, with 'Xm scouting vs Ym doing these searches yourself' beneath. The manual estimate is computed from the run's real counts with research-backed rates: 30s per web search (eye-tracking puts picking a result at ~9s, plus typing and reformulating; Mediative 2014, Granka et al.) and 60s per site opened (Nielsen Norman Group: average page visit just under a minute). The tooltip shows the formula, nothing invented.
steps: Start a search on the Scout tab and find the Time saving block under the reading deck while it runs.
Its line reads Xm scouting vs Ym doing these searches yourself, and both numbers should move with the run.
Hover the block: the tooltip shows the formula. Check it against the run's own searched and pages-read counts (30 seconds per web search, 60 seconds per site opened). Nothing invented.

tour.text: Start a run and watch under the reading deck for the Time saving block. Hover it: the tooltip's formula must match this run's own search and site counts.

items.title: Variety rotates industries
items.good: When a goal welcomes many industries, back-to-back scouts don't find the same field twice: the planner reads which industries past keeps already cover and points the new run at ones not yet represented.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a goal that welcomes many industries, for example companies that hire music business grads.
When it finishes, run the exact same goal again.
Compare the industries across the two runs in Finds: the second run should reach into fields the first did not, not refind the same industry twice.

tour.text: Run a variety-friendly goal from here twice in a row (each press spends a search).
Compare the two runs' industries: the second should cover ground the first did not.

items.title: Rescue reaches the floor
items.good: A run under 5 finds widens into other industries up to three times (fresh angles each round), and if still short re-reads every fetched page under a junk-only bar with honest low fit scores. Coming back with 3 is a Broken, not a shrug.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a narrow search where the specific ask runs dry.
Watch the progress card for the widening lines as it broadens into other industries, up to three rounds with fresh angles each time.
Count the finds: at least five, with rescue results carrying honest moderate fit bands, not inflated scores. Coming back with three is a Broken, not a shrug.

tour.text: Run a narrow goal from here and watch the progress card: you should see it widen rather than give up, and land at five or more finds with honest fit bands.

items.title: Deleted finds come back
items.good: Deleting a find drops it into 'Show recently deleted' at the foot of Finds (this device). Bring it back restores it exactly as it was, draft and status intact; Delete forever really removes it.

tour.text: Go to Finds and delete any find you don't mind moving (Delete on its row or detail).
Scroll to the very bottom: Show recently deleted lists what you just removed.
Press Bring it back. The find should return exactly as it was: same status, same draft.
If it came back whole, mark the item Works. Delete forever is the only true delete.

steps: In Finds, press Delete on a find you don't mind moving (on its row or in the detail view).
Scroll to the very bottom and open Show recently deleted: it should list what you just removed.
Press Bring it back: the find must return exactly as it was, same status, same draft.
Delete forever is the only true delete; test it on a junk find only.

items.title: Tiles read as Scout
items.good: Grid tiles paint a soft pastel of the site's brand color with the logo or dog in the deepened color itself. No full-strength color blocks, and a find with no known color gets a pastel from the field deck, never a dead grey tile.
steps: Open Finds and switch to grid view with the Grid view button beside the filters.
Look at the tiles: each should paint a soft pastel of the site's brand color, with the logo or the Scout dog drawn in a deepened shade of that same color.
Fails: a full-strength solid color block, or a dead grey tile on a find with no known color (those should get a pastel from the field deck instead).

tour.text: Run a search first so there are fresh finds to work with: type a goal and press the cream Scout button (one run spends one search, so Scout will not press it for you).
Switch to Grid view with the toggle next to these filters and read the tiles: soft pastels with the logo in the deepened color. No full-strength blocks, no grey tiles.

items.title: Junk can't haunt the grid
items.good: Old imports that let FALSE/TRUE cells or bare ids through as names get scrubbed on load; anything left nameless moves to recently deleted (recoverable), so no more FALSE cards or id-titled tiles.
steps: Use an account that once imported a messy sheet, or import one now from the Manual tab's Import your outreach.
Open Finds and reload the page: the load-time sweep should have scrubbed old junk.
No card may be named FALSE or TRUE, and no tile may be titled with a bare id.
Scroll to the bottom and open Show recently deleted: anything left nameless should have been moved there, recoverable, not destroyed.

tour.text: Scan the list and the grid: no FALSE cards, no id-titled tiles. Old import junk is scrubbed the moment this tab loads.
Nameless rows are not destroyed: they land in here, recoverable with Bring it back.

items.title: Job hunts hit careers pages
items.good: A job/internship search shows 'Adding the careers pages of N employers Scout already knows' once the company index has matches, and finds point at employers' own sites instead of LinkedIn/Handshake walls. The list grows itself: every organization any search finds joins it. Needs supabase/company_index.sql run once.
steps: Precondition: supabase/company_index.sql has been run once on the project; ask whoever owns the database if unsure.
On the Scout tab, pick a job project (Work Opportunities works) and run an internship or job search.

Watch the progress card for: Adding the careers pages of N employers Scout already knows. It appears once the company index has matches; a brand-new database may need a couple of runs to grow the list, since every organization any search finds joins it.
Open the finds: they should point at employers' own sites, not LinkedIn or Handshake walls.

tour.text: With a job project picked above, run a search from here and watch the progress card for the careers-pages line.
The finds should point at employers' own sites, not walled boards.

sections.title: The application desk
sections.blurb: Applying well is half the product now. Every item here is about the Applications tab and its kits.

items.title: Only real prospects reach the desk
items.good: The Applications tab holds things you APPLY to. People (coordinators, professors, contacts) never appear automatically, and a school name in the organization field alone does not qualify a find.
steps: Open the Applications tab on an account whose pipeline includes networking contacts (people, not postings).

Scan the list: every row should be something you apply to. Any bare person (a coordinator, a professor) that arrived automatically is a fail. A school name in the organization field alone does not qualify a find.
Now add one by hand: open Finds, click a find's name to open its detail view, and press Track as application.
Switch to Applications and confirm it now appears in the list.
Reopen the same detail view and press Untrack application (the same button, relabeled). Confirm the row leaves Applications.

tour.text: This is the Applications tab. Everything here should be something you APPLY to. Scan for any bare person who arrived automatically: that is a fail.
Now prove hand-tracking works. Go to Finds and open any find by clicking its name.
In the detail view press Track as application, check it appears on the Applications tab, then press Untrack application and check it leaves. If both held, mark the item Works.

items.title: Organized by your projects
items.good: The toggles mirror your own structure: one chip per project (with counts), and picking a project reveals its categories as a second row. Filtering never loses anything; All brings it back.
steps: Open the Applications tab. Under the header sits one chip per project, each with a count, starting with All.
Click a project chip: the list filters to that project, and when it has categories a second row of smaller category chips appears underneath.
Click a category chip and confirm the list narrows again.
Add the project chip counts up: they must equal the All count, and no application may vanish entirely while filtering.
Click All and confirm everything comes back.

tour.text: These chips mirror your own structure: All first, then one chip per project with its count.
Click a project chip: its categories appear as a second row of smaller chips. Click one to narrow further.
Check the arithmetic: the project counts must add up to All, and pressing All must always bring everything back. Then mark the item.

items.title: Deadline-first rows
items.good: The list is ordered by parsed deadline (soonest first, red under a week, 'no deadline found' honest when absent), one application per row across the screen.
steps: Find a real posting online whose text states a deadline (apply by a date). Copy the whole description.
Open the Applications tab and press Paste a posting (top right of the header). Paste the text, pick a project, and press Build my application.
When it lands, check its row: the deadline leads the row as a date with a days-left line, turns red when under a week, and sorts above rows with no deadline.
Rows with no parsed date must show 'set deadline' rather than inventing one.
Confirm rows run one per line across the full width of the screen, never two across.

tour.text: Press Paste a posting up here, paste a real job description that states a deadline, pick a project, and press Build my application.
When the prospect lands, its row should lead with the parsed date and days-left, red under a week, sorted above undated rows.
Rows without a date say 'set deadline', and every row runs full width, one per line. If all that held, mark the item Works.

items.title: The kit walks you through
items.good: Opening a prospect is a full-screen, numbered walkthrough: (1) point of contact and your materials, (2) a cover letter tailored to THIS posting with minimal edits and bracketed fill-ins, (3) know-them research with interview prep, plus Open posting up top.
steps: Open the Applications tab and press My application on a row built from a real posting.

The kit opens full screen with Open posting at the top. Step 1, Your point of contact and your materials: press Copy next to the contact email and paste it somewhere to confirm it copied, then click your resume row and confirm it downloads.

Step 2, Your cover letter, tailored to this posting: read it as YOUR letter lightly edited, with bracketed spots left for facts only you know. (No letter showing? Save a base cover letter under Templates, Application materials first.)
Step 3, Know them before you apply: check the company facts, Before you apply points, and Interview prep questions cite real, checkable things about the organization.

tour.text: Press My application on any row to open its kit.
Step 1: copy the point of contact, download your resume, and check your links carry Copy buttons.
Step 2 is your cover letter tailored to this posting: your words with the smallest edits, brackets left for facts only you know.
Step 3, Know them before you apply: real facts and interview prep, plus Open posting up top. If every piece held up, mark the item Works.

items.title: Paste a posting, get a prospect
items.good: Pasting a whole job description (Applications or Manual) parses role/org/contact, researches the organization, and lands the prospect in Finds and Applications with its kit ready.
steps: Copy a whole real job posting from the web, including any contact name it mentions.
Open the Manual tab, scroll to Paste a posting, paste it, pick the project and category it should land in, and press Build my application.
When it finishes, open Finds and then Applications: the same prospect should be in both, carrying the right role, organization, and any stated contact.
Press My application on it and confirm the kit opens with research about the organization.

tour.text: This is the Paste a posting box on the Manual tab. Paste a whole real job description, pick where it should land, and press Build my application.
Open Finds: the prospect should carry the right role, organization, and any contact named in the posting.
Then check Applications: it is there too, and My application opens a working kit. If so, mark the item Works.

items.title: Schools bring scholarship leads
items.good: When the target is a school or degree program, the kit's research includes real scholarship or aid leads with links, never fabricated ones.
steps: Copy the program page text for a real masters program and build it: Manual tab, Paste a posting, Build my application (or use an existing school prospect).
Open Applications, press My application on it, and scroll to the end of Know them before you apply.
For schools a 'Scholarships worth a look' section should appear there, each lead with a link and a why line.
Click every scholarship link: each must resolve to a real page and relate to that school or program. An invented scholarship is a broken, not a needs-work.

tour.text: Build an application for a masters program first: paste the program page here and press Build my application.
Open its kit from Applications and scroll to the end of Know them before you apply.
Scholarships worth a look must list real, linked scholarships. Open each link; anything invented is Broken. Then mark the item.

items.title: Files persist and match
items.good: A file added during one application (a song, a portfolio) is kept and pulled up automatically the next time it fits, audio for playlist/music submissions, documents broadly. Files are grouped by kind in Templates > Application materials.
steps: Open a kit (Applications, My application) and in Step 1 under Your files press '+ Add a file this application needs (kept for next time)'. Add a song or a document.
Reload the page, then open a DIFFERENT application of the same kind (another music submission for audio, another job for documents): the file should surface in its files list by itself.
Open Templates, switch to the Application materials page, and confirm the file is listed there, grouped by kind.
Remove it there, reopen a kit, and confirm it stays gone.

tour.text: Open any kit and look at Step 1, Your files: the dashed '+ Add a file this application needs' control stores a file for next time.
Add a file, reload the page, then open ANOTHER kit of the same kind: the file should already be offered there.
Templates, Application materials lists the same files grouped by kind; removing one there must remove it from kits too. Then mark the item.

items.title: Compare charts with your ranks
items.good: Compare view shows a type group side by side, location, the group's own criteria (tuition, paid, remote, deadline…), fit, status, with a My-rank column you type into that reorders the list.
steps: Open the Applications tab and click a project chip whose group holds several prospects.
Press Compare in the List / Compare toggle at the right end of the chip row.
The table shows My rank first, then Application, Location, the group's own criteria columns (tuition, paid, remote, deadline, whatever the goal asked), Fit, and Status.
Type 1, 2, and 3 into three My rank boxes: the rows reorder to follow your ranks.
Clear one rank and confirm that row falls back into deadline order.

tour.text: Pick a project chip with several prospects, then press Compare at the right end of this chip row.
The first column is My rank: type 1, 2, 3 into three rows and watch the order follow you.
Clear one rank: that row falls back to deadline order, and the criteria columns should be the group's own asks. Then mark the item.

items.title: Tailoring keeps your voice
items.good: Tailoring (in a kit or Templates > Application materials) proposes the SMALLEST spot edits: your sentences survive, truly incompatible passages are flagged for YOU to resolve, and suggestions never point at text that isn't in your letter.
steps: Open Templates and switch to the Application materials page.
In the 'Tailor it to a job' card, paste your real cover letter and a real job description, then press Find the smallest changes.
Walk the suggestions one at a time: count them (a handful, not a rewrite) and check each highlighted original passage really exists in your letter.
Press Keep my original on one suggestion and confirm your sentence survives untouched in Your tailored letter at the end.
Truly incompatible passages must be flagged 'Doesn't fit this job' for YOU to resolve, never silently replaced.

tour.text: Scout is opening Templates. Switch to the Application materials page with this toggle.
Find the Tailor it to a job card: paste your real letter and a real job description, then press Find the smallest changes.
Step through the suggestions: each shows the passage highlighted in context with a Why. Use this change applies it; Keep my original must leave your sentence alone.
Count the edits (a handful is right) and check every highlighted passage really is in your letter. Then mark the item.

items.title: Deadlines edit in place
items.good: Clicking the deadline spot on any Applications row (or its 'set deadline' placeholder) opens the native date picker right there. A hand-set date wins over the parsed one and the list re-sorts immediately; clearing it falls back to the parsed date.
steps: Open the Applications tab. On any row, click the deadline block at the left edge (or its 'set deadline' placeholder): the native date picker opens right there.
Pick a date within the next week: the row shows the date with red days-left and the list re-sorts immediately.
Click the deadline again and clear the date in the picker: the parsed deadline (or 'set deadline') returns and the row re-sorts back.

tour.text: Each row leads with its deadline. Click the date (or 'set deadline') on any row: the date picker opens in place.
Pick a date next week: red days-left, and the list re-sorts at once. Clear it and the parsed date (or 'set deadline') comes back. Then mark the item.

items.title: Kits can skip the letter
items.good: 'Don't need a cover letter' on a kit's cover-letter step removes that section for THIS application only (the next step renumbers), with a small link to bring it back. The choice sticks across reopens.
steps: Open a kit (Applications, My application). To the right of the Step 2 heading 'Your cover letter, tailored to this posting' press 'Don't need a cover letter'.
The section disappears and 'Know them before you apply' renumbers to step 2. Close the kit and reopen it: still gone.
A small '+ Add the cover letter section back' link sits where the section was; press it and the section returns.
Open a different application's kit: its cover letter step must be untouched.

tour.text: Open a kit and find the small 'Don't need a cover letter' link beside the Step 2 heading.
Press it: the section goes, the next step renumbers, and closing and reopening the kit keeps it gone.
'+ Add the cover letter section back' restores it, and other applications must be untouched. Then mark the item.

items.title: Research cites real sources
items.good: Know-them ends with Sources and recent news: the actual pages the research read, linked with their real titles. Every link resolves and relates; none are invented.
steps: Open a kit (Applications, My application) and scroll to the end of 'Know them before you apply': a 'Sources and recent news' list shows the pages the research read, linked with their real titles.
Open every link: each must resolve and be about this organization.
A dead or unrelated link is a fail; an invented one is a broken.

tour.text: Open a kit and scroll to Sources and recent news at the end of the research step.
Open each link: real page, real title, really about them. Then mark the item.

items.title: Links read as links
items.good: In the kit's files column, saved links sit under their own 'Your links (what forms ask for)' heading with LINKEDIN / EMAIL / WEBSITE labels and copy buttons, never as unexplained bare values among the files.
steps: First make sure links are saved: Templates, Application materials page, fill the Your links card (Website, LinkedIn, Contact email, Phone).
Open any kit: in Step 1 under Your files, the links sit under their own heading 'Your links (what forms ask for)' with WEBSITE / LINKEDIN / EMAIL labels and a Copy button on each.
A bare unexplained value mixed in among the files is a fail.

tour.text: Check your links are saved first: Templates, Application materials, the Your links card.
Now open any kit: under Your files the links appear beneath 'Your links (what forms ask for)', each labeled with a Copy button. Then mark the item.

items.title: Research talks to you, briefly
items.good: Know-them research says 'you' and 'your', never your name in the third person, and stays short: a couple of company facts, 2-3 before-you-apply points, 3-4 prep questions, one scannable line each.
steps: Open a kit: Applications tab, My application on any row.
Read 'Know them before you apply' out loud. It must talk TO you, saying you and your, never your name in the third person.
Count the content: a couple of company facts, 2 to 3 Before you apply points, 3 to 4 Interview prep questions, each a single scannable line. Walls of text are a needs-work.

tour.text: Open any kit with My application.
Read the research: it should say you and your, never your name, and stay short: a couple of facts, 2 to 3 Before you apply points, 3 to 4 prep questions, one line each. Then mark the item.

sections.title: Bringing in your own lists
sections.blurb: Most people arrive with a spreadsheet already. This is where they decide whether Scout is for them.

items.title: Import a messy sheet
items.good: It handles merged cells, blank rows, notes in odd places, and inconsistent headers without falling over.
steps: Open the Manual tab, scroll to Import your outreach, and press Import a file.
In the Import your outreach history window press Choose a file and pick a REAL tracking sheet, the messier the better: merged cells, extra tabs, checkbox columns, stray notes.
If the sheet has several tabs, check the 'Which tabs hold your contacts?' chips and untick tabs that are not people (Senders, Config).

Answer any questions under 'What Scout understands' until the percentage is high, then press Review columns: every real column should map to a sensible field, junk columns to nothing. Fix any misses with the dropdowns.
