Press Import N rows, then open Finds: rows carry the sheet's names, emails, and companies, nothing dropped or scrambled, and no TRUE/FALSE junk.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window for you (Manual tab, Import your outreach).
Press Choose a file and pick a REAL tracking sheet, the messier the better: merged cells, extra tabs, checkbox columns.

Untick any non-people tabs under 'Which tabs hold your contacts?', answer the What Scout understands questions, then press Review columns: every real column should map somewhere sensible, junk columns to nothing.
Press Import N rows, then open Finds: rows should carry the sheet's names, emails, and companies, and no TRUE/FALSE junk. If so, mark the item Works.

items.title: Columns read right, or ask
items.good: It works out which column is a name, an email, or a company. When it is unsure, it asks rather than guessing.
steps: Make a small sheet with odd header names (say who, their mail, org) plus one column Scout cannot possibly guess.
Import it: Manual tab, Import your outreach, Import a file, Choose a file.
Scout reads the headers itself; when unsure it asks under 'What Scout understands' instead of guessing. Answer a question and watch the percentage climb.
Press Review columns and confirm name, email, and company each mapped to the right field; the unguessable column should map to nothing. Fix any misses with the dropdowns and finish the import.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window (Manual tab).
Choose a file with odd header names. Scout matches headers itself and asks under What Scout understands when unsure; asking is correct behavior, silent guessing is not.
Press Review columns: name, email, and company must each be mapped right. Fix any with the dropdowns, finish the import, then mark the item.

items.title: Import a Sheets link
items.good: Pasting a link imports the rows, and a link that is not shared gives a clear message about permissions.
steps: In Google Sheets open your sheet, press Share, set access to Anyone with the link as Viewer, and copy the link.
In Scout: Manual tab, Import your outreach, Import a file. Paste the link into the field under 'Or paste a link' and press Read link.
Pick the tabs, answer any questions, press Review columns to check the mapping, then press Import N rows.
Open Finds and confirm the contacts landed with their real details.
Now paste the link of a sheet that is NOT shared and press Read link: you must get a clear message about sharing permissions, not a spinner or a cryptic error.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window: it lives on the Manual tab under Import your outreach.
In Google Sheets, press Share, set access to Anyone with the link as Viewer, and copy the link.
Paste it under 'Or paste a link' and press Read link. Pick the tabs, press Review columns to check the mapping, then Import N rows.
Open Finds and confirm the contacts landed with real details. Then try a PRIVATE sheet's link: a plain message about sharing is a pass, a cryptic failure is not.

items.title: Accents survive
items.good: Names with accents or non-English characters come through intact.
steps: Make a tiny CSV with accented names (Jose with an accent, Zoe with a diaeresis, Renee) plus emails.
Import it: Manual tab, Import your outreach, Import a file, Choose a file, then Import N rows.
Open Finds and read the names: every accent intact, no garbled characters.
Press Draft on one of them and check the name is still intact inside the message.
items.tech: Related to a known issue elsewhere where accented spellings were treated as different people.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window. Import a small file with accented names.
Open Finds: the names must show their accents exactly, no garbled characters.
Press Draft on one of them: the accented name must survive into the draft too. Then mark the item.

items.title: Huge files don't hang
items.good: It either handles it or tells you the limit. It never spins forever.
steps: Build a sheet with several thousand rows: in Google Sheets or Excel, fill a name and an email column down 5,000 rows and export a CSV.
Open Manual, Import your outreach, Import a file, Choose a file, and pick it.
Time it: the button shows Reading… while it works. The app must either finish the import or state a limit plainly. A spinner that never resolves is a broken.
If it imports, open Finds and confirm the list still scrolls smoothly with the new rows.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window. Feed it a file with several thousand rows and time what happens.
While it reads, the Choose a file button shows Reading… It must end in an import or a plain limit message, never spin forever. Afterwards check Finds still scrolls smoothly. Then mark the item.

items.title: Bad files fail politely
items.good: A corrupt file, or a photo renamed as a spreadsheet, produces a clear message and no damage.
steps: Rename a photo so its name ends in .csv.
Open Manual, Import your outreach, Import a file, press Choose a file, and pick the fake CSV.
You should get a plain-English error inside the window, the app stays usable, and nothing was imported (check Finds).

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window. Press Choose a file and pick a photo renamed to .csv.
You should see a plain-English message, no crash, and no rows imported. Then mark the item.

items.title: Add a contact by hand
items.good: You can add someone manually with everything you know, and they behave exactly like a found result afterwards.
steps: Open the Manual tab and press Add a contact.
Type only the name of someone with a public presence and press Autofill the rest: fields fill from the public web, never invented, and blanks stay blank when nothing is found.
Pick the project it belongs to (or mint one with + New project…) and add them.
Open Finds: they appear like any other find. Press Draft on them and confirm a normal draft comes out, addressed to them.

tour.text: Scout is opening the Add-a-contact form for you (Manual tab).
Type only a name you know is public (an artist, a manager) and press Autofill the rest. Fields should fill from the public web, never invented.
Pick the project it belongs to (or mint one with + New project…) and add them.
Open Finds: they sit there like any find, and pressing Draft writes to them exactly like a scouted one. Then mark the item.

items.title: Junk cells never become contacts
items.good: Checkbox values like TRUE and FALSE never show up as names or LinkedIn handles, sentence-long notes are skipped instead of imported as people, and emails are found even when the email column was mislabeled.
steps: Make or use a sheet with a checkbox column (TRUE/FALSE values), a row holding a sentence-long note, and an email hiding in a mislabeled column.
Import it: Manual tab, Import your outreach, Import a file, Choose a file, Import N rows.
Open Finds: no row may be named TRUE or FALSE, and no note-sentence may have become a person.
Open a few imported rows and confirm the emails were picked up even where the column header was wrong.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window. Use a sheet with checkbox columns, a note row, and a mislabeled email column.
After importing, scan Finds: any card named TRUE or FALSE, or a note-sentence as a name, is a fail. Emails must be found even from mislabeled columns. Then mark the item.

items.title: Rows link back to the sheet
items.good: A contact from a linked Google Sheet has a small open-in-sheet arrow that opens the source spreadsheet scrolled to that person's row.
steps: Import a Google Sheet by link (Manual, Import a file, paste under 'Or paste a link', Read link) and tick 'Keep this sheet synced' before finishing.
Open the Spreadsheet tab: the synced sheet's contacts are listed there.
Click the small open-in-sheet arrow next to an imported contact: the source spreadsheet must open scrolled to that person's row, not the top of the sheet.
Try a contact from a different tab of the sheet to confirm the tab is right too.

tour.text: Precondition: import a Google Sheet by link here (Import a file, Or paste a link, Read link) and tick Keep this sheet synced.
Open the Spreadsheet tab and click the open-in-sheet arrow next to an imported contact: Google Sheets should open highlighting that exact row. Then mark the item.

items.title: Imported contacts stay private
items.good: After importing a spreadsheet, published business addresses (submissions@, booking@, info@) may help other accounts' searches, but a private individual's personal address (a gmail, a named person's work mailbox) never leaves your account.
steps: Import a sheet containing both a published role inbox (submissions@ or booking@) and a private personal address (a personal gmail): Manual, Import your outreach, Import a file.
Open Finds and confirm both contacts landed in your own pipeline with their addresses.
In a private window, sign in to a second account (a fresh throwaway signup, never the real Music Row Promo account) and run a search squarely in that niche.
The person with the private address must never surface there with that address. The role inbox being reused is acceptable; the personal one appearing for the other account is a broken.
items.tech: isBusinessContact gates what crosses into the shared index: role-style inboxes on non-freemail domains only.

items.title: Hand-adds research themselves
items.good: Right after adding a contact by hand, Scout quietly runs the same public-web enrichment as Autofill: blank fields (role, outlet, link, location) fill in and the 'Added by you' placeholder becomes one real factual line when the web has one. Nothing invented; blanks stay blank when nothing is found.
steps: Open Manual and press Add a contact. Type ONLY the name of someone findable (an artist, a manager). Do NOT press Autofill the rest; just pick a project and add them.
Open Finds and watch their card for a minute: role, outlet, link, and location should quietly fill in from the public web.
The 'Added by you' placeholder line should become one real factual line when the web has one.
Check each filled fact against the web: anything invented is a broken. If nothing was found, blanks staying blank is correct, not a failure.

tour.text: Scout is opening the Add-a-contact form (Manual tab). Type only a findable name, skip Autofill the rest, pick a project, and add them.

Open Finds and give it a minute: role, outlet, link, and location should fill in quietly, and the Added-by-you line should become one true fact. Blanks staying blank is fine; invention is Broken. Then mark the item.

items.title: Sheet data lands on finds
items.good: After importing a real tracking sheet, the rows carry the sheet's company, email, phone, and links, not blanks with placeholder text. Kaitlyn's current pipeline shows imported rows with empty contact fields, so this is under investigation.
steps: Open Manual, Import your outreach, Import a file, and re-import the real tracking sheet.
Before finishing, press Review columns: does each sheet column map to the right field (company, email, phone, links)? Fix any misses with the dropdowns.
Press Import N rows, then open a few imported finds and compare them against the original sheet row by row.
If the mapping looked right but fields still landed blank, mark Broken and put the sheet's exact column names in the note.

tour.text: Scout is opening the import window. Re-import the real sheet and press Review columns before finishing: every column should map to the right field.

Open a few imported finds side by side with the sheet: company, email, phone, and links must have landed, not blanks. If the mapping was right but fields are blank, mark Broken with the column names in the note.

items.title: Postings file where you choose
items.good: Both Paste-a-posting boxes (Manual and Applications) offer project and category pickers; the built prospect lands exactly there, not in whatever project was active.
steps: Open Manual and scroll to Paste a posting. Paste a posting and, in the two pickers, choose a project that is NOT your active one, plus a category.
Press Build my application, then check Finds and Applications: the prospect must sit under the project you picked, not whatever project was active.
Repeat from the Applications tab: press Paste a posting at the top right, pick a different project there, press Build my application, and confirm it files where you chose.

tour.text: This is Manual's Paste a posting box. Its pickers choose where the prospect lands: pick a project that is NOT your active one.
Build it, then check Applications: it must sit under the project you picked (its chip), not the active project.
Repeat with the Paste a posting button up here on Applications: same pickers, and it must obey them too. Then mark the item.

sections.title: Writing the messages
sections.blurb: The part users judge us on hardest. Read the drafts as if you were the person receiving them.

items.title: Drafts sound like a person
items.good: You would be willing to send it with light edits. It does not open with generic flattery or read like every other outreach email.
steps: Open Finds on the New tab and press Draft on five different people, one at a time.
Read each draft aloud (it appears right on the find, and collects under Drafts).
Count how many you would send with only light edits. Fewer than three of five is a needs-work.
Generic flattery openers or an interchangeable template feel fail a draft on the spot.

tour.text: Go to Finds and press Draft on five different people, one at a time.
Read each aloud. Would you send it with light edits? Under three of five passing is Needs work, and a generic flattery opener is an automatic fail. Then mark the item.

items.title: Two people, two different drafts
items.good: Swap the names between two drafts and it should immediately look wrong. If they are interchangeable, the personalisation is fake.
steps: Draft messages for two quite different people: Finds, press Draft on each.
Put them side by side (open the two finds in turn, or use the Drafts tab).
Mentally swap the recipient names: if either message would still read fine for the other person, the personalization is fake and this is a needs-work.
The specifics referenced (their outlet, their work) must belong to each person alone.

tour.text: Draft for two different people from Finds.
Open the two drafts side by side and swap the names in your head: if nobody would notice, the personalization is fake. Each draft should cite things only that person did. Then mark the item.

items.title: No unbacked claims
items.good: Every specific claim about their work traces back to something in the result, not to a guess.
steps: Take three drafted finds. Open each find's detail view, where its source links and Why it fits sit next to the draft.
Highlight every factual claim the draft makes about the person: their role, their outlet, the work it compliments.
Trace each claim to the find's linked sources or the person's own pages.
Anything specific-sounding that cannot be traced is a broken, not a needs-work.

tour.text: Open a drafted find: the draft sits alongside the find's own sources and Why it fits.
Highlight every claim in the message and hunt each one down in the linked sources. A claim you cannot trace is Broken. Repeat on three drafts, then mark the item.

items.title: Email long, DM short
items.good: The format matches the channel automatically, without you having to ask.
steps: Pick a find whose contact is an email address and press Draft: you should get a full email with a subject line.

Pick a find whose only contact is a social handle: the format picker beside the Draft button should already read a DM format (Instagram DM, LinkedIn message), and drafting gives a short note with no subject.
Compare the two: the DM must be noticeably shorter and looser than the email, without you asking for it.

tour.text: On a find with an email, Draft writes a full email with a subject line.

Now open a find with only a social handle: the format picker beside Draft should already show a DM format, and the draft comes out short with no subject. If the formats matched the channels on their own, mark it Works.

items.title: Edits teach your voice
items.good: After you rewrite a few drafts heavily, later drafts start closer to how you write.
steps: Open three drafted finds (Finds, Drafted tab). The message body is editable right on the find: rewrite each substantially in your own words (your openers, your rhythm, your sign-off) and click out so the edit saves.
Draft three NEW people (back on the New tab, press Draft).
Compare the fresh drafts to your rewrites: openers, rhythm, and sign-off should have moved toward yours. No movement at all is a needs-work.

tour.text: Open Finds, Drafted, and rewrite three drafts heavily in your own words, right in the message box on each find.
Now draft three new people from the New tab.
Read the new drafts against your rewrites: they should start noticeably closer to how YOU write. Then mark the item.

items.title: Coach reads your real messages
items.good: The advice quotes your real drafts and says something specific. Generic outreach tips are a needs-work.
steps: Draft at least three messages first (Finds, press Draft).
Open the Dashboard and scroll to Outreach advice, the 'Tailored to you' block.
Press 'Review my N recent drafts'.
Read the tips: each must quote or clearly reference something you actually wrote. Generic outreach tips with no tie to your drafts are a needs-work.

tour.text: You need a few drafts first: Scout coaches on YOUR messages, not a textbook. Draft three from Finds.
On the Dashboard, scroll to Outreach advice and press Review my recent drafts.
Every tip must point at something you actually wrote. Advice that could apply to anyone is Needs work. Then mark the item.

items.title: Follow-ups remember the first
items.good: The follow-up reads like a second message to the same person, not a fresh cold email.
steps: Draft a first message, then a follow-up.
Read them in sequence as the recipient would.

tour.text: You already have sent messages, so we can test with a real one. This is your Sent list; each card has a Follow up button.
Scout is drafting a follow-up to your first sent message now. When it lands on the card, check it reads like a second note to the same person, referencing your first message, not a fresh cold email.
Nothing has been sent yet, so first get one message out: run a search here, draft a message on a find, and send it (or Mark as sent).
Once it shows in Sent, press Follow up on the card and check the draft reads like a second note to the same person, not a fresh cold email.

items.title: Redraft a batch
items.good: Redoing several drafts together produces the same quality as doing them one at a time, and nothing gets mixed up between people.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a search and draft several finds so the Messages list at the bottom holds around ten drafts.
In the 'Refine your messages' box above them, type one instruction (for example: make these shorter and more casual) and press Apply.
Read every rewritten draft: same quality as drafting one at a time, still addressed to the right person with that person's details.
Any detail that crossed wires between people (one person's work praised in another's message) is a broken.

tour.text: Draft a batch first: run a search here and draft several finds so the Messages list at the bottom fills up.
Scroll to Refine your messages above the drafted messages, type one instruction, and press Apply.
Now read EVERY draft: right person, right details, no mixed-up facts between people. One crossed wire is Broken. Then mark the item.

items.title: Application writer is submittable
items.good: Given a real job posting, the cover letter and answers are specific to that posting and to the applicant.
steps: Copy a real internship posting and build it: Manual tab, Paste a posting, press Build my application.
Open Applications and press My application on it. Read Step 2, the tailored cover letter, as if you were the hiring manager.
It must be specific to this posting and to the applicant. Bracketed fill-ins are fine; boilerplate that would fit any job is a needs-work.

tour.text: Build one from a real internship posting: paste it here and press Build my application.
Open its kit from Applications and read the cover letter as the hiring manager would: specific to the posting and to you, or it is Needs work. Then mark the item.

items.title: House rules respected
items.good: No em dashes anywhere, no filler openings, no exclamation marks unless you wrote them.
steps: Collect ten drafts: Finds on the Drafted tab, or the Messages list at the bottom of the Scout tab.
Scan each for the house rules: no em dashes anywhere, no filler openings like 'I hope this finds you well', no exclamation marks you did not write yourself.
One slip across the ten is a needs-work; a repeating pattern is a broken.

tour.text: Open your drafted messages: Finds, Drafted tab.
Scan ten drafts for em dashes, filler openers, and exclamation marks you didn't add. One slip is Needs work; a pattern is Broken. Then mark the item.

items.title: Pick the template per draft
items.good: On a find with two or more templates in scope, the Draft button grows a 'Best template (auto)' picker listing each template by kind and first words. Picking one drafts from that voice alone; auto still matches by format.

tour.text: You need two or more templates in scope first: on Templates' Outreach page, check the Where-it-applies picker on your templates covers this project.
Open any NEW find in Finds: next to Draft sits the source picker, reading Scout picks the best template.
Pick a specific template: its text previews under 'Starting from this template' before you commit. Draft, and the message should carry that template's voice. Then mark the item.

steps: Precondition: save at least two Outreach templates whose Where-it-applies scope covers the project you are testing (Templates, Outreach page).
Open a NEW find in Finds: next to the Draft button sits the source picker, reading 'Scout picks the best template'.
Open the picker: it lists each template by kind and first words, plus 'Write my own message'. Pick a specific template: its full text previews under 'Starting from this template' before you draft.
Press Draft: the message must clearly start from that template's voice, personalized for the person.
Set the picker back to 'Scout picks the best template' and draft another find: auto mode should match a template to the message format on its own.

items.title: One email link, not two
items.good: The find detail shows the address itself as the contact link; there is no separate Email chip repeating it (Call chip gone the same way).
steps: Open a find that has an email address (Finds, click its name).
In the detail view's contact rows, the address itself is the clickable contact link.
Confirm there is no separate Email chip repeating the same address, and no Call chip repeating the phone number either.

tour.text: Open any find with an email and look at its contact rows: the address itself is the link.
There must be no second Email chip repeating it, and no Call chip. If each contact detail appears exactly once, mark it Works.

items.title: Delete team templates
items.good: A shared template row has Delete: your own delete removes it from the library (and your local copy so sync can't resurrect it); an admin can delete anyone's. A non-admin deleting someone else's gets a plain refusal, not a broken row.
steps: On a team account, open Templates: the Shared templates banner shows you are on the team lens, and teammates' templates appear with their names.
Delete one of YOUR OWN shared templates with its Delete control, then reload: it must stay gone (sync must not resurrect your local copy).
As an admin or owner, delete a template someone else saved: allowed.
As a plain member, try deleting someone else's: you should get a plain refusal message, and the row must stay intact, not break.

tour.text: On the team lens, Templates is the shared library: teammates' templates carry their names.
Delete one of your OWN templates, then reload: it must stay deleted. The admin and non-admin checks need teammates' accounts; run those from the steps. Then mark the item.

items.title: Walkthroughs use your real account
items.good: A walkthrough checks what is on the account first: with messages already sent, the follow-up walkthrough goes straight to a real sent message instead of asking you to draft a first one from scratch.
steps: On an account with sent messages, press Walk me through it on Follow-ups remember the first: it should open Sent and use a real card.
On a fresh account, the same walkthrough should start from running a search instead.

sections.title: Sending
sections.blurb: The only part that touches a stranger's inbox. Mistakes here cost us our sending reputation, not just a bug report.

items.title: Connect Gmail
items.good: The connection completes on the live site and still works a week later.
steps: On the live site, open Profile and scroll to Send from your email.
Press Connect email, then Gmail, and finish Google's consent screen with a real Gmail account.
Back in Profile the card should read 'Connected as' your address, with the 'When you use a draft' choice underneath.
Prove it works: open a drafted find and press 'See it in Gmail'; the draft must appear in that Gmail account's Drafts folder.
Come back a week later and create a draft again: it must still work without reconnecting.
items.tech: If the Google app is still in testing mode, only listed test users can connect and their access expires after seven days, so this looks fine on day one and breaks quietly later.

tour.text: Open Profile and find Send from your email. Press Connect email, choose Gmail, and finish Google's consent screen.
The card should now read Connected as your address. Open a drafted find and press See it in Gmail: the draft must land in your Gmail Drafts folder.
The week-later half can't be walked through today: leave the item open and re-test in a week before marking it Works.

items.title: Connect Outlook
items.good: Same as Gmail, including for a work account with stricter settings.
steps: Open Profile, Send from your email, press Connect email, then Outlook, and finish Microsoft's sign-in with a personal Outlook account.
Confirm the card reads 'Connected as' your address, and that a drafted find's 'See it in Outlook' puts a draft in that mailbox.
If you have access to a work Microsoft account, repeat there: stricter tenant settings are exactly what this test is for. An admin-consent block must show a readable message, not a dead end.
Come back a week later and confirm the connection still works.

tour.text: Open Profile, press Connect email, and choose Outlook, then finish Microsoft's sign-in.
Check the card says Connected as your address, and that a drafted find's See it in Outlook lands a draft in that inbox. Repeat with a work account if you have one. Then mark the item.

items.title: Draft mode vs send mode
items.good: Whichever you choose, Scout does exactly that. In review mode nothing ever leaves without you pressing send.
steps: Open Profile, Send from your email. On the connected mailbox card, under 'When you use a draft', pick 'Create a draft I review'.
Go to the Scout tab's Messages list (the drafts from your last run). The one-click button on each email draft should now read 'Create Gmail draft' (or Outlook).
Press it, then check your mailbox: the message sits in Drafts, and your Sent folder shows nothing went out.
Switch the setting to 'Send automatically': the same button now reads 'Send from Gmail'. Careful: that really sends, so first set the draft's To to an address you own.
In review mode, nothing may ever leave without you pressing send in your own inbox. Anything in the Sent folder you did not send yourself is a broken.

tour.text: In Profile, the connected mailbox card has the choice 'When you use a draft'. Pick Create a draft I review (Scout is pointing at it; choose it yourself).
On the Scout tab's Messages list, the button on each email draft should now read Create Gmail draft. Press it, then check your mailbox: in Drafts yes, in Sent no.
Flip the setting to Send automatically and the button becomes Send from Gmail, which REALLY sends: point the To at your own address before trying it. Then mark the item.

items.title: One real send
items.good: It arrives, in the inbox rather than spam, and it looks right on a phone.
steps: Get a message drafted on a find (Draft button) if you don't have one already.
In the To bar above the subject, put an address you own on a DIFFERENT provider: sending from Gmail, use an Outlook or Yahoo address.
Press Send from Gmail on the draft.
Open that other inbox: it should be in the inbox (not spam or promotions) and read cleanly on a phone.

tour.text: You need something to send first. Type a goal and press Start scouting; Scout will find people to reach.
Pick a find and press Draft. Scout writes the message for you.
You already have drafts, so we'll send one of those. Open a draft card here.
In the To bar above the subject, replace the address with one YOU own on a different provider. Sending from Gmail? Use an Outlook or Yahoo address you can check.
Press Send from Gmail. (This really sends, which is the point of the test.) Then open that other inbox: the message should be in the inbox, not spam or promotions, and read cleanly on your phone.

items.title: Opt-out works via the client
items.good: Cold sends carry a List-Unsubscribe header, so Gmail and other clients show their own Unsubscribe control on the message; using it lands the address in the suppression table and Scout never emails it again. The message BODY carries no unsubscribe line or token URL, it reads like a personal note.
steps: Precondition: run the One real send test so a Scout message sits in an inbox you own on a different provider.
Open that message in Gmail: next to the sender, Gmail's own Unsubscribe control should appear (it comes from the hidden List-Unsubscribe header Scout adds to cold sends).
Read the body as a stranger: it must read like a personal note, with NO unsubscribe line and no token URL anywhere in the text. A visible unsubscribe line in the body is a fail.
Use Gmail's Unsubscribe control. If it opens the link version, you should land on a plain 'You're unsubscribed' confirmation page.
Back in Scout, try to send to that address again: Scout must refuse and say the person opted out.

items.title: Opt-outs actually stop mail
items.good: After someone opts out, no further message from that account can reach them, including scheduled and automatic ones.
steps: Unsubscribe one of your own test addresses first (see the opt-out item above).
In Finds, open the find with that address and press Send from Gmail: Scout must refuse with a message that this person opted out of your outreach.

Also try Schedule next to the Send button and queue a send a few minutes out: either it refuses immediately, or the queued message must never arrive (the sender checks the opt-out list before every send).
Check that inbox an hour later: still empty. Any delivery after an opt-out is a legal problem, not just a bug.

tour.text: Open the find whose address you unsubscribed. This is the Send button; press it yourself: the correct result is a refusal saying they opted out. (If the guard is broken it will really send, which is exactly what you are testing.)
Also try Schedule, right next to it, and queue a send minutes out: nothing may ever arrive in that inbox. Then mark the item.

items.title: Schedule a send
items.good: It goes out at the time promised, once, and not twice.
steps: Open a drafted find and set the To bar to an address you own on another provider.

Next to Send from Gmail press Schedule: the popover suggests a time and takes any date. Pick a time 25 to 30 minutes ahead and press Queue send (the queue is drained every 15 minutes, so give it that much slack).
The card now shows a green 'Scheduled' badge with the time.
Wait past the chosen time plus up to 15 minutes: exactly one copy arrives in that inbox, at roughly the promised time, and never a second one.

tour.text: Open a drafted find and put YOUR OWN other-provider address in the To bar first.
Press Schedule next to the Send button, pick a time 25 to 30 minutes out, and press Queue send. The card should show a Scheduled badge with the time.
Come back after the time, allowing up to 15 extra minutes for the queue: exactly one copy in that inbox is a pass; zero, or two, is Broken.

items.title: Sends respect their hours
items.good: Messages land during their working day, not the middle of their night.
steps: Pick a find in a far-away time zone (the card shows a 'their time' chip when Scout knows it, amber when outside their business hours) and put your own address in the To bar.

Press Send from Gmail while it is night for them: an amber notice should name their local time and a better time, with 'Wait for business hours' and 'Send anyway'. Choose Wait for business hours: nothing sends.
Open Schedule instead: the suggestion should read 'Suggested: next business hour in' their timezone. Queue it and confirm the arrival timestamp lands inside their working day.
Optional: in Settings under Sending, turn on 'Auto-schedule for the next business hour' and repeat: the send should quietly queue itself instead of asking.

tour.text: Find a card with an amber 'their time' chip (outside their hours) and put your own address in the To bar.
Press the Send button yourself: the amber heads-up should appear with Wait for business hours and Send anyway. Choose Wait: nothing sends. (Send anyway really sends.)
Schedule, next to it, should suggest their next business hour. Queue one to your own address and check when it arrives. Then mark the item.

items.title: Blank location falls back
items.good: A contact with no location still gets a reasonable send time rather than three in the morning somewhere.
steps: Open a find with no location and no 'their time' chip, or add one by hand (Manual, Add a contact) with the location empty and your own email as the address.
Draft it, then press Schedule next to the Send button.
The popover's note must read 'Suggested: 9am tomorrow, your time.' and the prefilled time must match it, never the middle of the night.
Queue it to your own address for the full proof, or press Cancel if the suggestion alone satisfies you.

tour.text: Open a find with no location (no their-time chip on the card). Draft it, then press Schedule next to the Send button.
The popover must say 'Suggested: 9am tomorrow, your time.' with the field prefilled to match. That is the fallback working. Cancel out and mark the item.

items.title: Repliers never get follow-ups
items.good: A real reply stops the sequence immediately.
steps: Send a real message to an inbox you own on another provider (the One real send flow).
After a send, Scout quietly queues an automatic follow-up several days out. From that other inbox, REPLY to the message the same day.
In Scout, the find should flip to Replied once the reply is picked up.
Watch the other inbox past the follow-up window (about a week): no follow-up may ever arrive. A reply must cancel the queued follow-up, not just restyle the card.
If a week is too long to wait, ask a developer to show the queued follow-up row was cancelled after the reply came in.

items.title: Disconnect stops the queue
items.good: Disconnecting revokes access and cancels anything waiting to send from that account.
steps: Queue two or three scheduled sends to your own address: on drafted finds press Schedule next to Send, pick times 30+ minutes out, and press Queue send. Each card shows a Scheduled badge.
Open Profile, Send from your email, and press Disconnect on the connected mailbox card.
The card should return to its Connect state (access revoked).
Wait past every queued time plus 15 minutes: nothing may arrive in your inbox, ever. A message that still sends after the disconnect is a broken.

tour.text: Queue a few sends to YOUR OWN address first: Schedule sits next to the Send button; pick times 30+ minutes out.
Now open Profile and press Disconnect on the mailbox card. Press it yourself: revoking access is the test.
Wait past the queued times plus 15 minutes: zero deliveries is a pass. Then mark the item.

items.title: Failed sends are visible
items.good: If a message fails, you can see it failed and why, and try again.
steps: Open a drafted find and set the To bar to an address that must bounce, like nobody@ followed by a made-up domain.
Press Send from Gmail (this really sends; the bounce is the point).
Within a few minutes the mailer-daemon bounce lands in your Gmail, and Scout should show a red Bounced badge next to the find's status.
Hover the badge: it explains the address bounced and suggests scanning for another contact.
Fix and retry: correct the To to an address you own, send again, and confirm the retry goes through.

tour.text: Put a guaranteed-bad address (nobody@ a made-up domain) in the To bar of a drafted find.

Press the Send button yourself (it really sends, and the bounce is the point). Within minutes the find should grow a red Bounced badge that explains itself and points at a fix. Correct the address and confirm a retry works. Then mark the item.

sections.title: Running on autopilot
sections.blurb: The riskiest feature we have, because it acts while nobody is watching.

items.title: Set up a recurring search
items.good: You can say what to look for and how often, and it runs on that schedule.
steps: Open the Scout tab and type a real goal into the goal box.
Below the goal, click the 'Search preferences' panel to expand it (its subtitle reads 'contact info, auto-find & emails'). You must be signed in; guests only see a sign-in note here.
Find the 'Auto-find:' row. Pick a cadence in the dropdown: 'every day' or 'every week'.
Optionally tick 'Auto-email me the finds' if you also want the digest email (needs a connected mailbox).
Press 'Turn on'. Note the fine print: each run counts as one search against your plan.
Confirm the confirmation line appears and the search now shows in the list at the bottom of the panel with its cadence and 'first run soon'.
Come back after the next scheduled time: the list entry should now read 'last <date>' and the new finds should be sitting in the Finds tab. Saved but never running is a fail.

tour.text: Type the goal you want Scout to re-run on a schedule.

Expand the 'Search preferences' panel below the goal. The 'Auto-find:' row inside it is the recurring-search control: pick 'every day' or 'every week', then press 'Turn on' yourself. Each run costs one search from your plan.

After you turn it on, the schedule appears in a list at the foot of the same panel with a 'Stop' button. Check back after the next run: the entry should say 'last <date>' and the finds should be in your Finds tab.

items.title: Digest reads well on a phone
items.good: It is scannable, the results are clear, and the buttons are easy to tap.
steps: Precondition: a signed-in account with a connected mailbox (Gmail or Outlook) and an auto-search turned on with 'Auto-email me the finds' ticked (Scout tab > Search preferences > Auto-find).
Wait for the next scheduled run, then open the digest email on a real phone, not a desktop mail client.
Check each find in it is scannable: name, role, and the reason it fits, without sideways scrolling.
Try to act on it one-handed: the 'Approve & draft' and 'Not a fit' buttons must be big enough to tap without zooming.

items.title: Approve from the email
items.good: Tapping approve or deny works straight from the email and confirms what happened.
steps: Precondition: a digest email from an auto-search (see the recurring-search item).
On a phone that is signed out of Scout, open the digest.
Tap 'Not a fit' on one find: the link should record the decision and show a confirmation page, with no sign-in demanded.
Tap 'Approve & draft' on another find: it should open the draft page for that find and the find should land in your pipeline as approved.
Later, sign in on a computer and confirm both decisions actually stuck in the Finds tab.

items.title: Stale links refused
items.good: Editing the link, or using a very old one, gets a clear refusal rather than acting on someone else's account.
steps: From a real digest email, copy the 'Not a fit' link (it points at /api/auto/action?t=... where t is a signed token).
Change any single character inside the t= value and open the edited link.
Confirm you get a plain refusal page and that nothing changed on the find. Any page implying the action happened is a broken.
Repeat with the 'Approve & draft' link (/auto/draft?t=...).
If you have a digest older than the token lifetime, open one of its links too and confirm the same polite refusal.

items.title: Nothing sends unapproved
items.good: There is no path, including a double click or a reused link, that gets a message out without human approval.
steps: Turn on an auto-search with the email digest (Scout tab > Search preferences > Auto-find > 'Turn on').
After a run, confirm the finds arrive in Finds as things to review, with drafts at most; nothing shows in the Sent tab that you did not send yourself.
In the digest, tap 'Approve & draft': confirm it opens a DRAFT for you to read, and mail only leaves when you press the send button on it yourself.
Tap the same 'Approve & draft' link a second time and confirm you do not get a second copy queued; one find, one draft.
Double-click the send button on a draft in the app and check the Sent tab shows exactly one message for that contact.

items.title: Off means off
items.good: Pressing Stop on every schedule under Search preferences halts the feature immediately: no further runs, no new finds or digests, and no searches spent after the moment you stop them.
steps: Open the Scout tab and expand 'Search preferences'. The badge on the panel shows how many schedules are on (for example '2 on').
In the list at the bottom of the panel, press 'Stop' next to every scheduled search.
Confirm the list empties and the 'on' badge disappears.

Wait past the next time it would have run (next morning for a daily one). Confirm no new finds appeared in Finds, no digest email arrived, and your search allowance on the Billing tab did not tick down.

tour.text: Expand 'Search preferences' under the goal box. The badge shows how many scheduled searches are on.

Press 'Stop' beside every entry in the list at the bottom of the panel. That is the off switch; there is no separate autopilot toggle. Then wait past the next scheduled run and confirm nothing new arrived and no search was spent.

sections.title: Getting smarter over time
sections.blurb: We promise Scout improves. That promise needs to be visible, and one part of it needs a decision before launch.

items.title: Decide on the self-editing job
items.good: This is a decision, not a test. A nightly job reads how people are rating results and then edits our own live code and publishes it, with no human reviewing the change first.
steps: Know what you are deciding about: a nightly cron at /api/cron/auto-tune reads real search outcomes and, past a confidence gate, edits one tunable clause in lib/discover.ts and commits it straight to main with no human review; Vercel deploys it from there.
Agree as a team whether that stays on for launch day. The safer variant is proposing the change for a person to approve.
To turn it off: remove the GITHUB_AUTOTUNE_TOKEN environment variable in Vercel (the job then skips itself). Removing SCOUT_OWNER_EMAILS also disables it.
To spot a change: every applied edit is written to the auto_tune_log table, emailed to the owner's connected mailbox, and shows on the dashboard News card as 'Scout got better'.
To undo one: open the GitHub commit linked in the log entry and revert it. Make sure everyone on the team has done this once on a dry run.
items.tech: The nightly tuning job commits directly to the main branch through a scoped access token. Its safety net is that it may only replace the contents of specific named clauses, not arbitrary code.

items.title: Deny reasons group sensibly
items.good: Three differently worded versions of wrong industry count as one reason, not three.
steps: Open the Finds tab and pick three finds you do not want.

On each, press 'Deny', then answer the 'Why pass?' prompt with slightly different wordings of the same idea: pick the 'Wrong industry' chip once, and type variants like 'wrong industry for me' and 'industry is wrong' the other times.
Open the Dashboard tab (You view) and find the 'Why you pass' chips in the learned section.
Confirm the differently worded versions are counted together as one reason with a count of 3, not three separate chips of 1.

tour.text: Run a search first so there is something to pass on.
Open a find you do not want and press 'Deny'. Answer 'Why pass?' with 'Wrong industry'. Do the same on two more finds, but type your own wording of the same idea, like 'wrong industry for me'.
Now check the Dashboard's 'Why you pass' chips: the three differently worded passes should count as ONE reason with a count of 3.

items.title: Better within one session
items.good: After a round of passes and edits, the next batch is noticeably closer to what you want.
steps: On the Scout tab, run a real search and write down your own score out of ten for the first ten results.
Work the batch: press 'Deny' with a reason on the misses, star or draft to the hits, and edit one draft into your own words.
Run the same goal again from the Scout tab (the category picker remembers it).
Score the next ten the same way. The second score should be clearly higher; no visible movement after a full round of feedback is a needs-work.

tour.text: Type your goal here and run it, then score the first ten results for yourself, out of ten.
Work the batch in Finds: Deny the misses with a reason, star or draft to the hits.
Run the same goal again and score the new top ten. The score should move up within the same session.

items.title: Comparisons stay anonymous
items.good: Any people like you statistic is an average over enough other users that nobody can be identified.
steps: Two gates exist: the 'people like you' cohort in /api/community-stats returns nothing unless at least 5 OTHER users share the use case (MIN_COHORT in app/api/community-stats/route.ts), and the dashboard section 'You vs the community' does not render at all under 50 total users.
Ask a developer to show the API response for an account in a cohort smaller than 5: the cohort field must come back null, not a small average.
Have them confirm the endpoint only ever returns averages and counts, never emails, names, or per-user rows.
On the dashboard of a small deployment, confirm the 'You vs the community' section is entirely absent rather than showing thin numbers.

items.title: Insights matches reality
items.good: The numbers on it agree with what you can count yourself.
steps: Open the Dashboard tab, You view. The stat band across the top is what you are auditing (Finds, Messages sent, Searches run, Drafts written, and so on).
Verify 'Finds' by opening the Finds tab, setting the source toggle to 'Both' if it is showing, and comparing the total.
Verify 'Messages sent' against the Sent tab's count.
If 'Hours saved scouting' is showing, check it is roughly finds x 15 minutes plus drafts x 10 minutes, rounded to hours.
Any mismatch you can reproduce after a reload is a broken.

tour.text: This stat band is the claim under test. Pick two numbers from it, say Finds and Messages sent.
Now count for yourself: the Finds total here (set the source toggle to Both if it is visible) must equal the dashboard's Finds stat, and the Sent tab count must match Messages sent.

sections.title: Keeping track of the pipeline
sections.blurb: The dashboard's whole job is to be trusted. A confidently wrong number is worse than no number.

items.title: Dashboard numbers are real
items.good: Every count on the dashboard can be verified by hand against the actual rows.
steps: Open the Dashboard tab, You view, and pick three stats from the band, for example Finds, Messages sent, and Drafts written.
Count Finds yourself on the Finds tab with the source toggle on 'Both'.
Count Messages sent on the Sent tab and Drafts written on the Drafts tab.
Reload once and re-compare. Any mismatch, however small, is a broken.

tour.text: Pick three numbers from this stat band, say Finds, Messages sent, Drafts written.
Count the real rows behind them: Finds here (source toggle on Both), Sent on the Sent tab, Drafts on the Drafts tab. Every count must match the dashboard exactly.

items.title: Statuses stick
items.good: Marking something as sent or replied survives a reload and shows up on the dashboard.
steps: Open the Finds tab and open a find.
Use the status pill dropdown at the top of the card to set it to Sent; on a find already sent, use 'Mark replied'.
Change two or three finds this way, note the counts on the status tabs along the top, then reload the page.
Confirm every status survived the reload, the status-tab counts still agree, and the Dashboard stat band moved to match.

tour.text: Open a find and change its status with the status pill at the top of the card. Do a few, and note the counts on these status tabs.
Reload the page: every status change must survive, and the Dashboard numbers must have moved with them.

items.title: List and grid views
items.good: Both views show the same items, sort the same way, and stay usable with hundreds of rows.
steps: Open the Finds tab on an account with a lot of finds (a few hundred if you have them).
Find the two small icon buttons just left of the 'Filters' button above the list: the lines icon is List view, the squares icon is Grid view (hover shows the names).
Flip between the two and confirm both show the same items in the same order, and the status-tab counts do not change.
Scroll a long way in each view and confirm neither stutters or drops rows.
Change the sort, flip views again, and confirm the order matches in both.

tour.text: The two icon buttons just left of Filters switch List and Grid view. Flip them: same items, same order, same counts in both, and both must stay smooth with hundreds of rows.

items.title: Lists survive reloads
items.good: A saved list is still there after a refresh, and after signing in somewhere else.
steps: Precondition: the Lists tab is currently removed from the nav on purpose (the 'lists' entry is commented out of the TABS list in app/app/page.tsx until the feature is good enough to ship). Saved lists still exist in state, but there is no way to reach them in the UI.
Mark this item blocked until a developer re-adds 'lists' to TABS and its nav item.
Once it is back: open the Lists tab, save a list from a project or category, reload the page, and confirm the list is still there.
Sign in on a second device and confirm the same list appears there too.

items.title: Deep links land on the right row
items.good: Clicking a link through to a spreadsheet row opens the right row, not the top of the sheet.
steps: What actually exists: on the Manual tab under 'Import your outreach', each entry in 'Synced sheets' has a 'What it reads' button, and inside it an 'Open the sheet' link that opens the source spreadsheet.
Open that link for two different synced sheets and note where Google Sheets lands you: it opens the sheet, not a specific row.
If the promise is landing on the RIGHT ROW, this feature does not appear to be built; flag it to a developer rather than hunting for a control that is not there.
Until then, judge the item on what exists: the link must at least open the correct spreadsheet without an error.

tour.text: Under 'Import your outreach', expand a synced sheet's 'What it reads' and press 'Open the sheet'. Note where it lands: today it opens the sheet itself, not the row, so if the row-level promise matters, this is a gap to flag.

items.title: Write results to Sheets
items.good: The rows land in the right sheet, in the right columns, without overwriting anything.
steps: Preconditions: connect Google on the Manual tab ('Connect Google (reads private sheets)' under Import your outreach), and link a Google Sheet to a project via 'Paste a sheet link'. Only Google Sheets links can be written to; public CSV links are read-only.
In the 'Synced sheets' list, tick 'Allow edits' on that sheet. Scout shows a preview of what it will write before the box actually turns on; read it.
Change a couple of find statuses in that project, then give it a moment and open the real spreadsheet.
Confirm the status column updated on the matching rows (as New, Drafted, Sent, Replied, Passed) and new finds were appended at the bottom.
Most important: confirm every cell you did NOT expect Scout to touch is byte-for-byte untouched, including formulas and formatting on other columns.

tour.text: Everything for this test lives here: 'Connect Google (reads private sheets)', 'Paste a sheet link', and once a sheet is synced, the 'Allow edits' checkbox on its row. Tick Allow edits, read the preview it shows, then change some statuses and check the real sheet: statuses updated, new rows appended, and nothing else touched.

items.title: Pass reasons become one-tap
items.good: After you type a custom reason for passing on a find, it appears as a tappable chip next time, most-used first.
steps: Open the Finds tab, open a find you do not want, and press 'Deny'.
At the 'Why pass?' prompt, type your own reason (keep it under 60 characters; longer text stays free-text and never becomes a chip).
Deny a second find: your custom reason should now be a tappable chip beside the built-in ones (Wrong industry, Wrong role or level, and so on).
Use it a few times, add another custom reason, and confirm the most-used chips sit first.
Note the chips are stored per browser, so do not expect them on another device.

tour.text: Press 'Deny' on a find and TYPE your own short reason at the 'Why pass?' prompt instead of tapping a chip.
Deny another find: your reason should now be a tappable chip of its own, and the chips order by how often you use them.

items.title: Filter finds by source
items.good: The Finds tab has a Scout-found / Manual / Both toggle, defaulting to Scout-found, and the counts always match the list shown.
steps: Precondition: at least one Scout-found find and one hand-added one. If you have no manual ones, add one on the Manual tab with 'Add a contact'.
Open the Finds tab. Above the status tabs sits the source toggle, with counts baked into the labels: 'Scout-found N', 'Manual N', 'Both N'.
Confirm it defaults to Scout-found, and that flipping through all three changes the list and the counts together (Both must equal the other two added up).
Know the two intentional quirks: the toggle hides entirely when all your finds are one kind, and the Drafts and Sent views always open on Both.

tour.text: If you have no hand-added contacts yet, add one here so both kinds exist.
The Scout-found / Manual / Both toggle sits above these status tabs, counts in the labels. Flip through all three: list and counts must move together, and Both must equal the sum.

items.title: Lists read for outsiders
items.good: A list (say, Band members) shows everyone in plain English: not contacted yet, reached out with the date, replied, passed. Someone who has never used Scout can read it cold.
steps: Precondition: the Lists tab is currently removed from the app's nav on purpose (the 'lists' entry is commented out of TABS in app/app/page.tsx). Mark this blocked until a developer re-adds it.
Once it is back: open the Lists tab and create a list from one project or category.
Check the labels an outsider sees are the plain-English set: Not contacted yet, Draft ready, Reached out, Replied, Deciding, Passed.
Show the list to someone outside the team and ask who has been contacted; they should answer without help.
Change a find's status on the Finds tab and confirm the list updates by itself.

items.title: Dashboard sits on the field
items.good: The dashboard ground is a soft blended colour field (a fresh trio of tints dealt every time you open it, never repeating its lead), with film grain on the ground only and frosted translucent cards in one consistent surface style.
steps: Open the Dashboard tab, then leave to another tab and come back (or reload) several times: the colour field behind the page must deal a fresh trio of tints each open and never repeat its lead colour twice running.
Zoom in on the 'Start scouting' button and a stat card: text and buttons must be clean, with the film grain only on the background field.
Confirm no card is a plain solid white slab; they should all read as the same frosted translucent surface style.
Repeat once in dark mode.

tour.text: Reload or revisit this tab a few times: the colour field behind the page must change each open. Then look closely at the Start scouting button and a stat card: no grain speckle on text or buttons, no plain solid-white card.

items.title: Time saved shows on dashboard
items.good: The stat band shows hours saved (an estimate of manual sourcing plus drafting time), and it grows as finds accumulate.
steps: Check the dashboard band for 'Hours saved scouting'.
Sanity-check the number against roughly 15 minutes per find plus 10 per draft.

sections.title: Working as a team
sections.blurb: Built and reviewed, but never actually run with two real people. That has to happen before launch.

items.title: Invite and join
items.good: One person creates a workspace and invites, the other signs in, sees the invite, and joins successfully.
steps: On machine one: open the Team tab. If you have no workspace yet, use 'Name your company' and press 'Create company'.
In the invite box ('Invite teammates by email, paste several...'), enter the second person's email, pick a role in the dropdown (Admin, Editor, or Viewer), and press 'Invite all'.
Alternative path worth testing too: 'Get invite link' creates a /app?join=CODE link; copy it with 'Copy link' and send it. Only the emails you invited can join through it.
On machine two, with the second real account (not a second tab on the same laptop): sign in, open the Team tab, and confirm the banner 'You've been invited to <workspace>' with a 'Join' button.
Press Join and confirm the member list on machine one now shows both people.
items.tech: The repo notes say this flow has been type-checked and reviewed but never exercised with two signed-in users.

items.title: Share a project
items.good: The shared project's finds appear for everyone on it, and only for them.
steps: Know the model first: 'Share with team' gives the WHOLE workspace the project; there is no per-teammate sharing. The excluded person in this test must be an account outside the team.
As the owner: open the Projects tab, select the project, and press 'Share with team' (its tooltip reads 'Give the whole team this project and its finds').
As a teammate on the team lens: open the Finds tab and confirm the shared project's finds appear, each carrying the finder's name.
As an account that is NOT in the workspace: confirm the project and its finds are nowhere, even with a direct link to the app.

items.title: No double claims
items.good: The second person is told it is already taken. Nobody gets pitched twice by the same company.
steps: Both people open the Team tab and scroll to the shared project's find list.
On the same unclaimed find, both press "I'll take it" at nearly the same moment.
Exactly one should win: the winner sees "You're on this", the other sees "<name> is on this" and their button now reads 'Take over' instead of claiming silently.
Note 'Take over' is a deliberate act, not a bug; the test is that a claim is never silently double-held.
Refresh both screens and confirm both agree on the single claimant.

items.title: Viewers can't edit
items.good: Someone with view-only access cannot change anything, even if they know the direct link.
steps: As the owner: Team tab, invite a test account with the role dropdown set to 'Viewer', press 'Invite all', and have that account Join.
Sign in as the viewer and try real editor actions: change a shared find's status with its status dropdown on the Team tab, press "I'll take it" on a find, and try to invite someone.
Each attempt must fail; the invite box should not even be offered to a viewer.
Ask a developer to confirm the refusals come from the /api/team routes (server-side role checks), not just hidden buttons: replaying the request with the viewer's token must 403.

items.title: Removal cuts access instantly
items.good: A member can be fully removed from the team, and their access to shared projects ends the moment it happens, not when they next sign out. (Blocked today: the UI only supports demotion, cancelling pending invites, and deleting the whole company.)
steps: Reality check first: joined members only have a role dropdown (Co-owner, Admin, Editor, Viewer); the x button exists only on 'Pending invites' ('Cancel this invite'), and the only full cut is 'Delete this company'. Flag the missing remove-member control to a developer; this item stays blocked until it exists.

What you can test today: demote a member to Viewer while they are actively using the app, then have them try to change a shared find's status; the refusal should arrive on their next action, not their next sign-in.
Also test the invite path: press the x next to a pending invite and confirm that email can no longer join through the invite link.

If the team accepts company deletion as the removal story, test it on a throwaway workspace: 'Delete this company' (type the name to confirm) must cut every member's access to shared projects immediately.

items.title: No double emails from a team
items.good: If two teammates both have the same contact, only one message goes out.
steps: Precondition: this rests on the cross-user exposure cap (supabase/exposure.sql must have been run); ask a developer to confirm it is live before testing.
Both teammates add the same contact (same email address) to their own lists, either by hand on the Manual tab or via a shared project.
Teammate one drafts and sends to that contact from the app.
Teammate two then tries to draft and send to the same address; the send must be blocked or clearly warned, not silently delivered.
Have a developer show the exposure record for that contact incrementing once, not twice, and repeat the test through the auto-search digest path if the team uses it.

items.title: Codes can't be guessed
items.good: The codes are long enough not to be brute-forced, and repeated wrong attempts are slowed down.
steps: Directly testable: create an invite link on the Team tab ('Get invite link', giving /app?join=CODE). Sign in as an account that was NOT invited and open the link: it must refuse, because the link only admits emails on the invite list.
Look at the code itself: it should be long random characters, not a short word or a counter.
Press 'Reset' next to the link and confirm the old code stops working.
Ask a developer to confirm the code length and entropy in /api/team/invite-code, and whether repeated wrong join or company-code attempts are rate-limited server-side.

items.title: Shared templates work
items.good: A template saved for the team is usable by every member and edits do not clash.
steps: Both people switch to the team lens (pick the company in the sidebar).
Person one opens Templates and saves a template on the Outreach page; the banner explains templates saved here are published to the team's library.
Person two opens Templates and confirms it appears under 'From your team (N)', with person one's name on it.
Person two copies it (one-tap copy) and edits their copy; confirm person one's original is untouched, because edits happen on copies, not in place.
Person two tries to delete person one's shared template: only the author or an admin may; confirm the server refuses others.

items.title: Co-owners promote, not demote
items.good: The owner can set a member's role to Co-owner. Once someone is an owner, nobody (including the other owner) can change or remove their role.
steps: As the owner, change a teammate's role to Co-owner in the Team tab.
As that co-owner, confirm you can manage admins.
Try to change the other owner's role from either account, it must refuse.

items.title: Teammate finds show for all
items.good: Someone else's find appears in your list under the same project it was found in, and under All projects, with their name on it.
steps: Both accounts switch to the team lens by picking the company in the sidebar; the project must be one shared via Projects > 'Share with team'.
Person one runs a search on the Scout tab with that shared project selected in the sidebar project picker.
Person two opens the Finds tab with the same project selected and confirms the new finds are there, each labeled with person one's name ('Found by <name>').
Person two switches the project picker to All projects: still there. Switches to an unrelated project: not there.
Both people find the same person (run overlapping searches): the pipeline must show one row for them, not two.
items.tech: Searches publish through mergeFinds to /api/team/finds, which opens a shared project matching the local project's name on the first find. Rows dedup on (shared_project_id, dedup_key), where the key is name plus website host from lib/findKeys and is deliberately free of any project id. Two rows for one person means the key is being computed differently by two paths.

items.title: Late joiners see history
items.good: A person invited after the searching happened opens the project and sees the finds already in it.
steps: On a team whose shared project already holds finds: invite a brand-new account from the Team tab ('Invite teammates by email...' then 'Invite all').
Sign in as the new person, open the Team tab, and press 'Join' on the 'You've been invited to' banner.
Switch to the team lens (pick the company in the sidebar), open the Finds tab, and select the shared project.
Confirm the finds from before they joined are all visible, with the original finders' names on them, not just finds created after the join.
items.tech: This is what open_to_workspace is for: membership rows are written when a project is created, so a later joiner has none. Access falls back to workspace membership on projects Scout opened automatically. Projects shared by hand keep their picked member list on purpose, so a later joiner will NOT see those.

items.title: See who found what
items.good: On a shared pipeline, grid cards carry a small chip with the finder's name next to the status, and the list view says 'Found by <name>' instead of a generic label.
steps: Switch to the team lens: pick the company in the sidebar (rather than your personal account).
Open the Finds tab. In the 'Shared finds' banner, the 'Found by:' row of chips appears; leave it on 'Everyone'.
Switch to Grid view (the squares icon left of Filters) and scroll: every card found by a teammate must carry a small chip with the finder's name next to the status, without opening the card.
Switch to List view: teammate rows must say 'Found by <name>', not a generic label.

items.title: Team news reads like sentences
items.good: The dashboard news card says things like 'anna found 12 new prospects in My outreach' and 'anna sent 5 messages', never jargon like 'moved outreach: sent 1000'.
steps: Precondition: a teammate has done something since you last read the news (run a search in a shared project, sent messages).
Open the Dashboard tab. The News card sits near the top: a 'News' badge with 'since you last read this'.
Read every line as an outsider: they must be plain sentences like '<name> found 12 new prospects in <project>', never jargon like 'moved outreach: sent 1000'.
Press 'Read, close' and confirm the card goes away and stays away until something new actually happens.

sections.title: Paying for it
sections.blurb: Test with a real card on the live site. Test mode proves nothing about launch day.

items.title: Free tier matches the ads
items.good: The number of free searches in the product, on the pricing page, and in our documentation are all the same number.
steps: The number in the product is 3 free searches a month (FREE_LIMIT). Check it in three places and confirm they all say the same thing.
In-app: the Billing tab ('Plan & billing') on a free account must read 'You're on the free plan, 3 searches a month', and the meter '<used> / 3 searches'.
The run-out popup after the third search must say 'You get 3 free searches a month'.
The landing page pricing section and any setup docs must quote the same 3.
Then actually burn the allowance on a fresh account and count: the fourth search must be the one refused.
items.tech: Right now the code allows three free searches per month while the setup documentation says five. Pick one and make everything agree.

items.title: Buy Starter with a real card
items.good: Checkout completes, the plan shows as active, the allowance goes up straight away, and a receipt arrives.
steps: On the live site, open the Billing tab ('Plan & billing') and press 'Choose Starter' ($15 a month, 30 searches).
Complete the Stripe checkout with a real card.
Back in the app, without reloading or signing out: the Current plan panel must flip to 'Starter' and the meter to '<used> / 30 searches'.
Run one search and confirm the meter ticks to 1 / 30.
Confirm a Stripe receipt email arrives at the account address.

items.title: Buy Pro, upgrade from Starter
items.good: Both work, and upgrading gives the higher allowance immediately without double charging.
steps: On account one (free): Billing tab, press 'Choose Pro' ($30 a month, 60 searches) and complete checkout; plan shows Pro, meter shows / 60.
On account two (already Starter): Billing tab, press 'Upgrade to Pro'.
Confirm the allowance jumps to 60 immediately, mid-cycle.
Check the Stripe invoice: it must charge only the difference, not a second full month on top of Starter.

items.title: Running out reads as a next step
items.good: You are told what happened, when it resets, and how to get more. It should read like an offer, not a failure.
steps: On a free test account, run all 3 searches, then start a fourth.
The popup must be the offer-shaped one: 'You've used your free searches', explaining you get 3 a month, that it resets on the 1st, with Starter (30 searches, $15 / month) and Pro plainly offered.
Check the Billing tab meter agrees (3 / 3) and shows the reset date.
Read it as a new customer: it must feel like a next step, not an error. Raw technical wording or a dead end is a fail.
Repeat on a Starter account if you can: the message becomes 'You've hit your Starter limit' with an upgrade path.

items.title: Manage the subscription in-app
items.good: You can update a card, see invoices, and cancel without emailing us.
steps: On a paid account, open the Billing tab ('Plan & billing').
Press 'Manage subscription' in the Current plan panel; it opens Stripe's customer portal.
In the portal, do all three: update the card, open an invoice, and start (then abandon or complete) a cancellation.
Return to the app and confirm the plan panel still reflects reality. If the button is missing on a paid account, that is a broken.

tour.text: On a paid account, the whole test hangs off one button: 'Manage subscription' in the Current plan panel here. It opens Stripe's portal, where you update the card, view invoices, and cancel, all without emailing anyone.

items.title: Cancel keeps the paid month
items.good: Cancelling does not cut someone off the moment they click it.
steps: On a paid test account: Billing tab, 'Manage subscription', cancel the plan in the Stripe portal.
The portal must show access continuing until the end of the paid period, with the date.
Back in the app, confirm the plan still shows as active with its allowance, and searching still works.
Confirm the shown end date matches the paid-through date, and only after it does the account drop to the free plan.

items.title: Parallel runs can't cheat limits
items.good: Someone on their last search cannot get two by starting them together.
steps: Get an account down to its last search (check the Billing meter, for example 2 / 3 on free).
Open /app in two separate windows signed into that account, type a goal in each, and press the Scout button in both within a second of each other.
Exactly one run should proceed; the other must stop with the out-of-searches message, not run for free.
Reload the Billing tab and confirm the meter shows the limit exactly reached, never past it.

items.title: Access codes work once
items.good: It grants access on the first account and is refused on the second.
steps: On account one: Billing tab, 'Have an access code?' section, type the code into 'Enter code' and press 'Redeem'.
Confirm the success message ('You're all set, unlimited access unlocked') and that the plan panel now shows Unlimited with the Comp badge.
On account two: enter the SAME code and press Redeem.
It must be refused with a clear message, and account two's plan must not change.

items.title: Failed payments don't lock out
items.good: A card that fails gives a warning and a grace period, not an immediate wall.
steps: Ask a developer to simulate a failed renewal on a paid test account (Stripe test clocks or a failing test card on the next cycle).
While it is failing, use the app as that account: mid-work searching must keep working through the grace period, not hit an instant wall.
Open the Billing tab: the status badge next to the plan name should show the trouble (for example past_due) and the 'Manage subscription' portal should offer fixing the card.
Confirm a warning reaches the user (portal or email), and only after the grace period does the account drop to free limits.

sections.title: Trials, and the tools only we can see
sections.blurb: The way people meet Scout before signing up, and the back office we use to help them.

items.title: Try without an account
items.good: The trial link runs a real search, and the path into signing up is obvious once it runs out.
steps: Open a private window and go to the landing page; the try-it-free button leads to /app?try=1 (you can also open that address directly).
Confirm you land straight in the tool with no signup, and run a real search; results must be real finds, not a demo reel.
Keep searching until the guest allowance runs out.
The popup must read 'Create a free account to keep going' with a 'Create free account' button, and explain your finds and drafts are kept when you sign up.
Create the account and confirm the guest session's work came along instead of vanishing.

items.title: Admin is locked down
items.good: An ordinary account cannot see or reach the admin area, even with the direct link.
steps: Sign in as an ordinary (non-owner) account and go straight to /admin by typing the address.
You must get the access screen (sign-in prompt or a back-to-Scout page), never the Insights, Concierge, or Pricing content, and no flash of data before the refusal.
Try a deep link with a hash too, like /admin#concierge: same refusal.
Ask a developer to confirm the /api/admin routes check the owner allowlist server-side, by replaying an admin API call with the ordinary account's token and getting a 403.

items.title: Search on someone's behalf
items.good: It works, the results land in their account, and there is a record of who did it and when.
steps: Open /admin and switch to the concierge tab ('Concierge · seed finds for an account').
Pick the target: type the test account's email in the account field (it suggests existing accounts, and an email that has not signed up yet is allowed).
Enter a goal and run the search, or hand-add finds with the manual add form, then select the finds you want and press the seed button.
Confirm the confirmation ('Queued N finds for <email>') and that the account row now shows the queued count.
Sign in as that test account: the seeds must land on its next load or search.
Record of who and when: ask a developer to show the seed rows (they carry the queue time); if no admin identity is stamped on them, flag that gap.

items.title: Seeds reach only their person
items.good: Nobody else ever sees results prepared for someone else.
steps: In /admin#concierge, queue a distinctive find (an unmistakable name) for test account A.
Sign in as account B and load the app, run a search, and reload: the seeded find must never appear anywhere in B's Finds.
Sign in as account A and confirm it DID arrive there.
Repeat with an email that has not signed up yet, then sign that address up fresh and confirm the seeds arrive for it alone.

items.title: Delete really deletes
items.good: After deletion, none of that person's data is left anywhere.
steps: On a throwaway test account (never the real Music Row Promo account): open the Account tab and press 'Delete my account' in the Account card, then confirm.
Confirm you are signed out and the credentials no longer sign in.

Ask a developer to sweep every table for that user id, not just the profile: user_state, finds and shared team rows, auto-search schedules, exposure records, billing rows, mailbox tokens, and any seeded finds.
Anything left anywhere is a fail; also confirm the address can sign up fresh afterwards and starts truly empty.

items.title: Index gauge shows the flywheel
items.good: The admin page's Index tab shows how many people the shared index holds, how fast it is growing day by day, what share have an email or profile link, and the newest additions.
steps: Open the admin page and switch to the Index tab.
Run a search in the app, reload the tab, and confirm the numbers moved.
Before the database table is created it shows a friendly set-up note rather than an error, that is expected.

items.title: Pricing model responds to levers
items.good: The admin Pricing tab recalculates profit, margin, and breakeven instantly as you drag users, prices, usage, and costs, and the numbers agree with a hand check.
steps: Open the admin page, Pricing tab.
Set a simple mix (say 10 Starter at $10, nothing else) and hand-check MRR and profit.
Drag each slider and confirm the tiles, chart, and breakdown all move together.

items.title: Benchmarks read honestly
items.good: The Pricing tab's health card compares your numbers to the standard targets (70%+ gross margin, 2 to 5% free-to-paid conversion, every paid tier profitable) and its advice matches what the levers show.
steps: Open /admin and switch to the pricing tab.
In the levers, raise one paid tier's searches-per-month allowance until that tier's per-user economics go negative (watch the 'Per-user economics' panel).
Find the health card, 'How healthy is this? (vs industry standards)': it must flag the losing tier in plain language, not just colour a number red.
Cross-check its standards read honestly: 70%+ gross margin, 2 to 5% free-to-paid conversion, every paid tier profitable, and that its advice matches what the tiles and chart show after your change.

items.title: Design lab paints palettes
items.good: Make a palette has colour/range/punch sliders; click locks a swatch, double-click opens the colour wheel; Keep it and Save this palette store locally without shipping; Edit colours in the website editor paints the live frame per palette or per element.
steps: Open /admin and switch to the design tab.
In the 'Make a palette' panel, drag the colour, range, and punch sliders, then press 'Shuffle' a few times.
