Single-click one swatch to lock it, shuffle again: the locked colour must survive. Double-click a swatch: the colour wheel opens to edit it.
Press 'Keep it' and 'Save this palette (stays in this browser)', reload the page, and confirm the palette is still listed. Saving must never change the live app.
Switch to 'Website preview and editor', press 'Edit colours', click a saved palette to paint the whole frame, then click one element and recolour just that element.

items.title: Admin remembers your tab
items.good: Refreshing /admin stays on the same tab (the tab lives in the URL hash), instead of snapping back to Insights.
steps: Open Design, refresh: still on Design.
Share the URL with the hash: it opens on that tab.

items.title: Items point into the app
items.good: Expanding a checklist item shows 'Show me where in Scout'; clicking it makes the live pane jump to the right tab, scroll to the control the step means, and pulse a ring around it. On a phone it opens the app in a new tab instead.
steps: Open /admin and switch to the readiness tab (or open the shared /readiness page on a desktop).
Expand any checklist item and confirm it shows a 'Show me where in Scout' control.
Click it: the live app pane must jump to the right tab, scroll the control the step means into view, and pulse a ring around it.
Try items pointing at different tabs (an import item, a templates item) and confirm each lands on its own control, not just the top of the tab.
Repeat on a phone: instead of a pane, it must open the app in a new tab.

items.title: Algorithm health at a glance
items.good: Admin Insights shows the finding engine's vitals in plain words: finds discovered, keep rate, arrive-reachable rate, average fit, reply and bounce rates, finds per run and the 5-find-floor hit rate. Numbers match what you can hand-count for a small account.
steps: Open /admin#insights and scroll to the 'Algorithm health' section.

Confirm the vitals are all present in plain words: Keep rate (kept vs denied, of decided), Arrive reachable (found with an email or handle), Average fit with the share scoring 80+, finds per run, and 'Hit the 5-find floor' (runs delivering 5 or more).
Hand-verify against a small account you control: count its kept vs denied finds on the Finds tab and check the account's contribution is consistent with the panel's direction.
Reload after running a search on that account and confirm the numbers move rather than being frozen.

items.title: Real-search categories
items.good: Admin Insights categorizes the goals of real searches (internships, music promotion, press, investors...) with counts, distinct users, and example goals. Matches your gut read of the example goals; the old profile question is gone from Profile.
steps: Open /admin#insights and find the 'What people use Scout for' section.
Confirm each category row (internships, music promotion, press, investors, and so on) shows a count, distinct users, and example goals.
Read the example goals under two or three categories: your gut read of the goal text must match the category it was filed under.
Run an oddly worded search on a test account and confirm it lands in a sensible category on reload.
Open the app's Profile tab and confirm the old what-do-you-use-Scout-for question is gone; the panel now learns it from real searches.

items.title: Time on Scout, any window
items.good: The Time on Scout card toggles between totals and a per-day line graph, with presets (2 weeks, month, 3 months) and custom from/to dates. Windowed totals shrink sensibly and the lines match the bars.
steps: Open /admin#insights and scroll to the 'Time on Scout' card.
Flip its view toggle between totals and the per-day line graph.
Click each preset (2 weeks, month, 3 months) and confirm the totals shrink sensibly as the window narrows; a smaller window must never show a bigger total.
Set a custom from/to range with the date fields and confirm the graph and totals honor it.
Cross-check one person: their line's shape must match their bars for the same window.

items.title: Metrics measure choices
items.good: Admin > Metrics leads with decision quality: fit-score calibration (keep rate per bucket), avoidable vs taste denials, 15-minute re-runs, and keep rate per pass and per source. Pass/index numbers fill in from newly-stamped finds; the custom counter builder sits below.
steps: Open /admin#metrics.

The page must LEAD with decision quality: fit calibration first (keep rate per fit-score bucket, plus a 'no score' bucket). Higher buckets should keep more; a flat or inverted curve means the score is decorative.
Check the avoidable-vs-taste denials split: it shows the tuning headroom, with unclassified counted honestly.
Check the re-run panel ('Did the run satisfy, or get re-run?'): searches re-run within 15 minutes counted as dissatisfaction.
Check keep rate per source ('Do widening and reuse earn their keep?'). Pass and index numbers fill in only from newly stamped finds, so sparse early data is expected, not broken.
Confirm the custom counter builder sits below the decision metrics, not above them.

sections.title: Does it feel good to use
sections.blurb: We committed to being calm, clear, and accessible. Treat those as requirements, not aspirations.

items.title: First load on mobile data
items.good: The landing page appears quickly on a normal phone connection, not just on office wifi.
steps: Turn wifi off on a phone and load the site.
Time it.

items.title: Errors in plain English
items.good: Every error says what went wrong and what to do. No raw technical text, no silent nothing.
steps: Force a mid-search drop: start a search on the Scout tab, then turn wifi off; the message must say what happened and what to do, not spin forever or dump technical text.
Hit the limit: on a free account, run a fourth search and read the run-out screen as a non-technical user.
Feed the importer garbage: on the Manual tab, paste a private Google Sheet link into the importer and read the permissions message.
Let a session expire (or sign out in another tab) and press a button: the app must route you to sign in with an explanation, not fail silently.
Collect every message you saw; any raw error code, jargon, or silent nothing is a fail.

items.title: Keyboard-only works
items.good: You can tab through everything and always see where you are.
steps: Put the mouse away. From /app, Tab through the sidebar and confirm a visible focus ring on every stop.
Run a search end to end: Tab to the goal box on the Scout tab, type, and start the search from the keyboard.
On Finds, reach a find with Tab, open it with Enter, and trigger drafting from the keyboard.
In the draft editor, Tab between subject and body and reach the action buttons.
Also try the command palette (Cmd+K or Ctrl+K) as the fast path. Anywhere focus vanishes or a control cannot be reached is a fail.

items.title: Readable in light and dark
items.good: Nothing is grey-on-grey. Placeholder text is as readable as normal text.
steps: Switch your operating system to dark mode (macOS: System Settings > Appearance > Dark), and check the app followed; use the theme control under Settings > Display if you need to force it.
Click through every tab in the sidebar: Dashboard, Scout, Finds, Drafts, Sent, Manual, Applications, Spreadsheet, Projects, Templates, Profile, Team, Account, Settings, Billing.
On each, look for grey-on-grey text, and check placeholder text in inputs (the goal box, the invite box) is as readable as normal text.
Repeat the sweep in light mode. Note anything you had to lean in to read.

items.title: Reduced motion respected
items.good: Turning on reduce motion in the operating system calms the animations down.
steps: Turn on reduce motion: macOS System Settings > Accessibility > Display > Reduce motion; iPhone Settings > Accessibility > Motion > Reduce Motion.
Reload the landing page: large entrance and scroll animations must calm to simple fades or nothing.
Reload /app and watch the dashboard field, the cursor glow, and tab transitions: nothing should still be sliding or pulsing hard.
Turn the setting off and confirm the motion comes back, proving the app is actually reading it.

items.title: Works in real browsers
items.good: Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Safari on an iPhone all work, especially file uploads and previews.
steps: Run a short search, an import, and a draft in each.

items.title: Whole app on a phone
items.good: Navigation, long result lists, the draft editor, and checkout all work on a real phone.
steps: On a real phone (not a shrunken desktop window), sign in at /app.
Check the bottom bar runs Scout, Finds, Dashboard, Templates, More, and that More reaches everything else (Manual, Applications, Settings, Billing).
Run a search on the Scout tab and scroll a long results list; nothing should overflow sideways.
Open a find, draft to it, and edit the draft; the keyboard must not cover the editor.
Walk the Billing tab to a Stripe checkout screen (you can stop before paying).
Check safe areas: nothing important hidden under the notch or the home indicator.

items.title: 404s are helpful
items.good: A mistyped link shows a friendly page with a way back, not a default error screen.
steps: Type a nonsense address on the site.

items.title: Settings reads organized
items.good: Settings is grouped under App, Display, Account, Sending, and Your data instead of one long pile.
steps: Open the Settings tab from the sidebar.
Confirm the group headings appear in order: App, Display, Account, Sending, Your data.
Scan every card and decide whether it sits under a sensible heading; anything orphaned or misfiled is a needs-work.
Confirm it no longer reads as one long undifferentiated pile.

tour.text: Scroll this page top to bottom: the cards must sit under the group headings App, Display, Account, Sending, and Your data, each card filed somewhere sensible.

items.title: Brown only in the logo
items.good: Every screen wears the current warm palette consistently: cream and beige surfaces, brown brand CTAs, the dusty-blue denim rail, and the brown dog logo. No screen still carries the abandoned bright white-and-idea-colour look, which now lives only in the admin Design lab.
steps: Reality: the bright whites-and-idea-colours direction was reverted; the shipped design is the warm beige/cream/brown palette with the dusty-blue denim rail, and the bright look lives on only in the admin Design lab.
Click through every tab in light AND dark mode and confirm the warm palette is applied consistently: cream/beige surfaces, brown brand CTAs, dusty-blue rail and accents.
Confirm no screen still wears leftovers of the abandoned bright direction (stark white grounds with navy ink and per-tab idea colours).
The dog logo keeps its brown everywhere it appears.
If the team re-decides the direction, update this item before testing against it again.

items.title: Colour follows meaning
items.good: The active nav item is the one consistent slate pill on the denim rail, on desktop and in the phone bottom bar, in both modes; retired idea-colour pills appear nowhere outside the admin Design lab.
steps: Reality: the per-tab idea colours (navy/teal/magenta/violet pills) were retired with the design revert; the shipped sidebar is the dusty-blue denim rail whose active item is a single solid slate pill.
Click through every nav item and confirm the active state is the consistent slate pill on the rail, in light and dark mode.
Check the phone bottom bar marks its active tab the same consistent way.
If any tab still wears a leftover idea-colour active state, that is the fail now.
If the team revives per-tab colours, rewrite this item to the new map first.

items.title: Stage colour feels new
items.good: The Scout tab wears the same blended colour field as the dashboard (same deals, fresh per open), toggles and bullets read clearly on it, the results shelf below is plain white, and the cursor glow follows the mouse in the ground's own blended colour on both tabs.
steps: Open the Scout tab twice; the field changes.
Move the mouse around: the glow fades smoothly between colours and relaxes ~3s after the mouse rests.
Run a search: results sit on a white shelf.

items.title: Blobs and grain, ground only
items.good: The dashboard ground is white with soft blended colour blobs and film grain, and the grain textures ONLY the background: buttons, cards, and text are clean. The ground runs all the way to the footer.
steps: Look closely at the Start scouting button and stat card: no speckle.
Scroll to the bottom: no hard cutoff above the footer.

items.title: Dashboard is a mosaic
items.good: On a wide screen, sections pair up side by side sharing horizontal lines (learned + preferences, activity + what-makes-yours-special) with no lakes of empty space. Below 1280px everything stacks.
steps: View at full width and at laptop width.
A section sitting alone with a huge empty area beside it is a fail.

items.title: Empty sections hide
items.good: You vs the community does not render at all until enough people share the use case; no placeholder card promising future data.
steps: Know the gate: the 'You vs the community' section on the Dashboard renders only once the community holds at least 50 users.
On a deployment below that, open the Dashboard tab and scroll the whole page.
Confirm the section is entirely absent: no heading, no placeholder card promising future data, no empty frame.
If you can see a large deployment, confirm the section DOES appear there, proving the gate works in both directions.

tour.text: Scroll the whole page: with fewer than 50 users sharing stats, 'You vs the community' must not appear at all, not even as a placeholder promising future data.

items.title: Update banner dismisses
items.good: 'A newer Scout is ready' has a close button; dismissing keeps the current version for this session without reloading, and the banner returns on the next deploy.
steps: Trigger it: keep an app tab open while a new version deploys (any push to main deploys; or ask whoever is shipping to tell you when one lands).
The 'A newer Scout is ready' banner appears. Do NOT reload; keep working a moment to prove your state is intact.
Press its close button: the banner must go away and nothing may reload; your in-progress work stays put for the rest of the session.
After the NEXT deploy, confirm the banner comes back rather than staying dismissed forever.

parts.title: Set it up right before we go live
parts.intro: This part is mostly for whoever handles the technical setup, but it is written so anyone can follow along and check it has been done. Some items only need someone to say yes, this is done, and show you.

sections.title: Unfinished work sitting on a laptop
sections.blurb: Some finished work is not in the live site yet. Until it is, the live site is missing protections that already exist in code.

items.title: Decide on unpublished work
items.good: There are several changed files on a local machine that are not on the live site. Either they are finished and published, or they are set aside deliberately.
steps: Have the technical partner run 'git status' and 'git log --oneline -5' in ~/scout-web and read the output with you: any line marked M or ?? is work on the laptop that is not committed.

Open the Vercel dashboard, the scout-web project, Deployments, and compare the latest Production deployment's commit message with the newest 'git log' line. If they differ, committed work is also unshipped.
For each unpublished change, write one line: ship before launch, or parked deliberately with a reason.
This check is safe for you to sit in on, but reading git output is the technical partner's job.
items.tech: Five modified files plus two new ones exist locally and are not committed. Anything unpublished is also unbacked-up.

items.title: Publish security headers
items.good: The live site sends the standard protections that stop other sites impersonating or embedding us. They are written but not published.
steps: Go to securityheaders.com, enter https://scout-source.com, and press Scan.

Pass: the report shows Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, and Referrer-Policy present (the headers are written in next.config.js, so they exist once the site is redeployed).
If any of those show as missing, the code with the headers has not been published: ask the technical partner to push and redeploy, then scan again.
items.tech: The headers block in the Next config, including content security policy and strict transport security, is written but uncommitted.

items.title: Close the preview loophole
items.good: The feature that shows a preview of someone's website can currently be used by anyone on the internet to make our servers fetch any page they like, at our expense.
steps: In a private or incognito window (signed out), paste this address: https://scout-source.com/api/site-preview?url=https://example.com
Pass: you get an error or a sign-in message, never the example.com page itself.
Then sign in to Scout normally, open any find, and confirm the website preview still loads. Locked to strangers, working for users, is the pass.
items.tech: The site preview route is an open proxy until the signed preview token work is merged.

items.title: Know the rollback
items.good: Anyone on the team can put the site back to the previous version in a couple of minutes, without waking the developer.
steps: The rollback lives in the Vercel dashboard: open the scout-web project, click Deployments, find the previous Production deployment (the one before the bad one).
Open its three-dot menu and choose Instant Rollback (or Promote to Production). The site is back on the old version within a couple of minutes.
Write those exact clicks into a shared doc titled Rollback, including who has Vercel logins.
On a quiet day, have someone non-technical do it once for real, then roll forward again the same way.

items.title: Agree who runs this page
items.good: There are no automated tests in the project, so a person walking the core journeys is the only safety net we have.
steps: Name that person and agree which sections they run each time.

items.title: Fix the project description
items.good: The project's own readme still describes an early experiment with no accounts and no database, which will badly mislead anyone new.
steps: The file is README.md at the top of the scout-web repo. Today it still opens with 'Phase 0 spike' and says 'no auth, no database, one user', all of which is now false.
Ask the technical partner to rewrite it to describe today's Scout: accounts, Supabase database, teams, payments, scheduled jobs.
Pass: read the new README yourself and confirm nothing in it contradicts the product you use every day.

items.title: Decide on the extension
items.good: A decision is written down, build it after launch or drop it, so it stops being an open question.
steps: The idea: a Chrome extension the user runs on LinkedIn pages they already have open. They click it, it reads the profiles showing on their screen, sends that text (never their login) to Scout, and Scout ranks the people by fit to their goal, writes why each fits, drafts in their voice, and drops them into the pipeline deduped against the team.

Why it is the only workable route to LinkedIn's roster: the code runs in the user's own browser and own session, so Scout's servers never touch their credentials. This is how established sales tools do it.

What to weigh: it is still against LinkedIn's terms even in the browser, so it must stay click-initiated, human-paced, and limited to what is already on screen, never background crawling. It also needs Chrome Web Store review with minimal permissions, and LinkedIn changes their page layout often, so it needs ongoing upkeep.

Recommended timing: after launch. It is a separate codebase plus a store review, while the launch blockers are two-factor login, testing, and real users. Most of the work is already done, Scout's ranking and drafting engine is the hard part and it exists.
Rough build: a small extension that reads the visible page, one new signed-in Scout endpoint to score what it sends, and the existing engine behind it. Days, not weeks.
items.tech: Manifest v3 + content script, activeTab permission on click only (never all_urls background), new /api/extension/score endpoint reusing discover + draftFor.

sections.title: Keys and settings
sections.blurb: Scout talks to several outside services, each with its own key. Three of these settings quietly fall back to something unsafe if nobody sets them.

items.title: Live settings all filled
items.good: All keys and settings exist in the live environment, not only in the testing one, and the site has been republished since they were set.
steps: Open the Vercel dashboard, the scout-web project, Settings, Environment Variables. Filter to the Production environment.

Tick off each of these names (values stay hidden, the name being present is the check): NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, TAVILY_API_KEY, NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL, CRON_SECRET, ACTION_SECRET, UNSUBSCRIBE_SECRET, TOKEN_ENC_KEY, GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID, MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, STRIPE_PRICE_STARTER, STRIPE_PRICE_PRO, SCOUT_OWNER_EMAILS.
Any name missing from Production is a fail, even if it exists for Preview or Development.
After adding or changing any of them, go to Deployments, open the latest Production deployment's three-dot menu, and click Redeploy. Settings only take effect on the next publish.

items.title: Signing secrets set
items.good: Three separate features sign links to prove they came from us. If any is left unset, it falls back to a value that is written in the code itself, which means anyone could forge those links.
steps: The three names are ACTION_SECRET (signs the approve links in digest emails), CRON_SECRET (protects the scheduled jobs and backs up the preview links), and UNSUBSCRIBE_SECRET (signs unsubscribe links). If unset, the code falls back to values written in lib/autoSearch.ts, lib/previewToken.ts, and lib/unsubscribe.ts that anyone can read on GitHub.
Open the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Settings, Environment Variables, Production, and confirm all three names exist.
Ask the technical partner to confirm each value is a long random string (30 plus characters), not a word or a reused password.
Redeploy afterwards from the Deployments tab so they take effect.
items.tech: The unsubscribe secret, the email action secret, and the cron secret each fall back through weaker options down to a hardcoded string.

items.title: One site address everywhere
items.good: Every place that needs the site address points at the real domain. A wrong one breaks sign-in with Google and puts broken links inside sent email.
steps: The right value is https://scout-source.com in every one of these places.
Vercel, Settings, Environment Variables, Production: NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL must both read https://scout-source.com (the technical partner can reveal the values).
Supabase dashboard, Authentication, URL Configuration: Site URL is https://scout-source.com and the redirect list includes it.

Quick proof from outside: sign in with Google on the live site and confirm you land back on scout-source.com, and check a link inside any Scout email points at scout-source.com, not localhost or a vercel.app address.
items.tech: Three separate address settings are read in different parts of the code.

items.title: Rotate every shared key
items.good: If a key was pasted into a chat, a document, or a screenshot, it is replaced and the old one is switched off at the provider.
steps: List every place a key may have been pasted: chats, docs, screenshots, this checklist's history. Be honest, this is an amnesty not an audit.

Rotate each shared key at its own provider: Anthropic console (API Keys), Tavily dashboard, Supabase (Project Settings, API), Stripe (Developers, API keys, roll key), Resend (API Keys). Each provider has a create-new then delete-old flow.
Put the new value into Vercel, Settings, Environment Variables, Production, and redeploy.
Prove the old key is dead: the technical partner makes one call with the old value and shows you the rejection. Rotation without revocation is not done.

items.title: Admin list is correct
items.good: Only the right people can see the admin and insight screens, and the list is reviewed when someone joins or leaves.
steps: The admin list is the SCOUT_OWNER_EMAILS environment variable: Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Settings, Environment Variables, Production.
Have the value revealed and read each email address out loud. Every address on it can open scout-source.com/admin and see every account's data.
Remove anyone who does not need that, save, and redeploy from the Deployments tab.
Put a calendar note to re-read this list whenever someone joins or leaves.

items.title: Access codes accounted for
items.good: Every free-access code that exists was deliberately created, and we know how to switch one off if it leaks.
steps: The codes live in two environment variables: COMP_CODES (personal free access) and COMPANY_COMP_CODES (whole-company free access), in Vercel, Settings, Environment Variables, Production.
Have the values revealed and write down each code and who was given it.
To kill a leaked code, delete it from the variable, save, and redeploy. Note that in the same doc so the off switch is not a mystery later.

items.title: Key-owner page exists
items.good: If one person is unavailable, someone else can still rotate a key or reach a provider account.
steps: Make one shared doc with a row per account: Google (OAuth for Gmail and Sheets), GitHub, Supabase, Vercel, Stripe, Resend, Anthropic, Tavily.
For each row: who owns the login, who is the backup person, and where its API key gets rotated (the console page name is enough).
Pass: someone other than the primary owner can read the page and know exactly where to go if a key must be replaced on a Saturday.

sections.title: The database is fully set up
sections.blurb: Eleven separate setup scripts exist. Each one that has not been run silently switches a feature off. Nothing warns you, the feature just quietly does nothing.

items.title: Back up first
items.good: A snapshot exists from immediately before any setup script is run.
steps: On the paid Supabase plan: open the Supabase dashboard, the production project, Database, Backups, and confirm a backup dated today exists before any script is run.
On the free plan there is no Backups page: the technical partner takes a manual export (pg_dump, or Database, then the export option) and tells you the file name and where it is stored.
Also click Download a backup on the Admin page's Index tab at scout-source.com/admin, which saves the shared index as a dated JSON file.
Do not let anyone run a setup script until you have been shown the backup file or the dashboard entry from today.

items.title: All setup scripts run live
items.good: Every one has been run, and someone can show you the list with each ticked off.
steps: The scripts are the .sql files in the supabase folder of the repo. Every one is safe to run twice.

Open the Supabase dashboard for the production project, SQL Editor, New query. Run RUN-ME-catchup.sql first and RUN-ME-missing-tables.sql second (paste the whole file, press Run): together they cover the fixes found missing on the live database.

Then run each remaining file the same way, ticking it off: teams.sql, fix-profile-saving.sql, exposure.sql, subscriptions.sql, auto_searches.sql, guest_searches.sql, concierge.sql, people_index.sql, company_index.sql, scheduled_sends.sql, unsubscribes.sql, sheets.sql, search_history.sql, push_subscriptions.sql, admin_config.sql, allow_personal.sql, auto_tune_log.sql, pdl_cache.sql, readiness.sql.

Verify: in the same SQL Editor run: select table_name from information_schema.tables where table_schema = 'public' order by 1; and confirm the list includes workspaces, target_contacts, subscriptions, guest_searches, people_index, and scheduled_sends.
Pasting and running is safe for you to do yourself; reading the verification list with you is the technical partner's job.
items.tech: Teams, profile saving, subscriptions, exposure, unsubscribes, guest searches, auto searches, scheduled sends, sheets, tuning log, concierge. Missing subscriptions means nobody is metered and everyone gets unlimited use. Missing unsubscribes means opt-outs are accepted and then ignored. Missing exposure means the anti-spam cap does nothing. Missing profile saving means nothing a user enters persists.

items.title: Users can't see each other
items.good: This has been tested by actually trying it, not by reading the rules.
steps: Your half: sign up a fresh throwaway account (never reuse Music Row Promo or your own) in a private window and confirm it sees zero of your projects, finds, or profile.

The technical partner's half: open the Supabase dashboard, Database, Tables, and show you that every table in the public schema has the RLS badge (row level security) switched on. Any table without it is a fail.
Then have them show one failed attempt for real: signed in as the throwaway account, query another user's profiles row and get zero rows back.
Pass is the failed read, not a verbal assurance that the rules look right.

items.title: Backups on, restore practised
items.good: Automatic backups run, and somebody has actually restored one at least once so we know the process works.
steps: Open the Supabase dashboard, production project, Database, Backups. Pass for the first half: a schedule is shown and the newest backup is dated within the last day (this requires the paid plan; the free plan shows nothing here).
For the restore: have the technical partner restore a backup into a scratch project (never over production) and show you real data inside it, for example your own profile row.
Write the restore steps and how long it took into the rollback doc.
The restore practice is strictly a technical partner task.

items.title: Test and live split
items.good: Development work cannot touch real customer data.
steps: Ask the technical partner to put two values side by side: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL from Vercel (Settings, Environment Variables, Production) and the same name from the .env.local file in ~/scout-web on the laptop.

Pass: the two URLs contain different project identifiers. Identical URLs mean development experiments run against real customer data, which is the current known state, so expect this to fail until the split is done.
If they match, this pairs with the AT LAUNCH split-the-databases item; do not mark this one done on a promise.

items.title: Index table exists live
items.good: The supabase/people_index.sql script has been pasted into the Supabase SQL editor and run. Until then, searches work normally but nothing compounds and the admin Index tab shows its set-up note.
steps: Open the Supabase SQL editor for the production project.
Paste the whole people_index.sql file and run it (safe to run twice).
Run one search in the app, then confirm the admin Index tab shows a count above zero.

items.title: Re-run the teams script
items.good: The script has been run again since those changes went in, and a company's location field saves without an error.
steps: Open the Supabase dashboard for the production project, SQL Editor, New query.
Paste the whole of supabase/RUN-ME-catchup.sql from the repo and press Run (it contains the current teams.sql plus the open_to_workspace and workspaces.location fixes; safe to re-run).
In Scout, open Profile, the company page, type a location, and save. An error here means the script did not take.
Have a teammate confirm they can see a shared project someone else searched under.
items.tech: supabase/teams.sql gained an open_to_workspace column on shared_projects, a location column on workspaces, and a redefined is_project_member() that lets an open project be read by any member of its workspace. Every statement is idempotent, so re-running the whole file is safe. Until it is run, team find sharing silently does nothing and saving a company location fails on the missing column.

items.title: Index backs up in one click
items.good: Admin > Index has Download a backup: the whole table lands as a dated JSON file. Open it and spot-check a few records against the Index view.
steps: Sign in to scout-source.com as an account listed in SCOUT_OWNER_EMAILS and open the Admin page, then its Index tab.
Click Download a backup. A dated JSON file should land in your downloads.
Open the file and spot-check three records against what the Index tab shows on screen: same names, same details.
Pass: file downloads, opens, and matches. Safe for you to do yourself.

sections.title: Email that actually arrives
sections.blurb: Sign-in codes come from us through a mail provider. Most failures here happen in a settings screen, not in the code.

items.title: Own mail provider wired
items.good: The built-in sender allows only a handful of messages an hour and drops the rest without an error, which on launch day looks like a completely broken signup.
steps: Open the Supabase dashboard, production project, Authentication, Emails, SMTP Settings.

Pass: Enable custom SMTP is on, Host is smtp.resend.com, Port 465, Username resend, Sender email no-reply@mail.scout-source.com, Sender name Scout. This is all documented in supabase/AUTH-SETUP.md in the repo.
Proof from outside: sign up a throwaway account and confirm the code email's From address is no-reply@mail.scout-source.com, not a supabase.io address.

items.title: Domain records verified
items.good: The mail provider shows the sending domain as verified, with all four records in place.
steps: Open the Resend dashboard, Domains, and click mail.scout-source.com.

Pass: the domain shows Verified, with all records green: the DKIM TXT record, the MX record, the SPF TXT record, and the DMARC record (they live in Cloudflare DNS; the exact values are written in supabase/AUTH-SETUP.md).
If any record shows failed, fix it in Cloudflare exactly as Resend displays it, then click Verify DNS Records again. Safe for you to check; editing DNS is the technical partner's job.

items.title: Templates carry the code
items.good: Both the signup and password reset emails show the six-digit code. The default templates do not, they show a link instead.
steps: Trigger both emails and look at what arrives.

items.title: Code is six digits
items.good: The app's box accepts exactly six characters, so any other length makes signing up impossible.
steps: Count the digits in a real received code.

items.title: Somebody watches bounces
items.good: A named person checks the mail provider for bounces and complaints, because that is the first sign of a delivery problem.
steps: Bounces and complaints show in the Resend dashboard, Emails: each sent message lists its status, and Bounced or Complained is the warning sign.
Name the person who opens that page, agree the rhythm (daily for launch week, weekly after), and put it on their calendar.
Agree the trigger: more than a couple of bounces in a day means stop and investigate before sending more.

sections.title: Guardrails on cost and spam
sections.blurb: The largest open risk in the product. Some features cost us money every time they run, and a set of them can currently be triggered by anyone at all.

items.title: Close the free-trigger features
items.good: Fifteen features that cost us money each time they run can currently be used by anyone who knows the address, with no account, no limit, and no counting. Somebody could run up a large bill from a script.
steps: Your spot-check: in a signed-out private window, paste https://scout-source.com/api/site-preview?url=https://example.com and confirm you get an error, not the page.

The technical partner's check: with no sign-in, call the money-burning endpoints under scout-source.com/api (draft, discover, deep-scan, application-kit, cover-letter, meeting-prep, read-website, read-company, enrich-contact, parse-profile, and the rest of the AI routes) and show you each answers 401 or asks for sign-in.
Anything that runs a search or an AI call for an anonymous stranger is a fail, except the guest trial path which is deliberately open but capped.
Treat this as the top cost risk of week one; get the demonstration, not the assurance.
items.tech: Drafting, redrafting, follow-ups, advice, deep scan, website and company reading, PDF reading, profile parsing, meeting prep, application writing, category and example goals, starter plans, and tuning prompts all lack authentication, metering, and rate limiting.

items.title: Hard caps at the providers
items.good: Even if something goes badly wrong in our code, the providers stop serving us before the bill becomes serious.
steps: The paid providers are Anthropic (Claude calls), Tavily (web searches), Vercel (hosting and job runtime), Supabase (database), and Resend (email).
Anthropic console: Settings, Limits, set a monthly spend limit and an email alert below it.
Vercel dashboard: team Settings, Spend Management, set a hard stop amount and an alert.
Supabase: organization Billing, keep the spend cap on (or set one after upgrading to Pro).
Tavily and Resend: confirm the plan's included quota is the effective cap and note what happens when it is hit.
For every alert, confirm the email goes to a person who will act the same day, and say who that is.

items.title: Trial can't run up costs
items.good: The no-account trial is capped per person per day, and the cap is switched on.
steps: Precondition: supabase/guest_searches.sql has been run in the Supabase SQL Editor (the cap counts in that table; without it, metering falls open).
In a signed-out private window open https://scout-source.com/app?try=1 and run searches back to back. The cap is 3 per day per connection.
Pass: the fourth attempt is refused and asks you to create an account, and the block still holds after closing and reopening the browser the same day.

items.title: Know what limiting does
items.good: Everyone knows that the current protection only slows down one very fast caller and is not a real quota.
steps: Have the developer explain the limitation in plain terms and decide whether it is enough for our expected volume.

items.title: Readers can't aim at us
items.good: Features that fetch a web address the user provides refuse addresses that point inside our own infrastructure.
steps: Have the technical partner demonstrate, not describe: feed the website-reading features an internal address and show the refusal.

Concrete probes: http://localhost, http://169.254.169.254/, and a decimal-IP disguise, sent to the site preview and the read-website autofill (the guard lives in lib/pageText.ts and is covered by tests).
Pass: every probe is refused with an error; any fetched content from a private address is a fail.
This one is genuinely technical; your role is to watch the probes fail.

items.title: Spend-spike alert exists
items.good: A simple threshold that emails somebody. It does not need to be clever, it needs to be read.
steps: Cheapest real version: Vercel team Settings, Spend Management, add an alert threshold well below the hard stop; and Anthropic console, Settings, Limits, add an email alert below the monthly cap.
Point both alerts at an inbox a named person reads daily.
Test one for real: set a temporarily tiny threshold, trigger normal usage past it, confirm the email arrives, then set the real threshold.

sections.title: The scheduled jobs actually run
sections.blurb: Three jobs run on their own in the background. Two of them run several times an hour, which not every hosting plan allows.

items.title: Plan allows the cron schedule
items.good: Sending runs every fifteen minutes, automatic searching every ten, and tuning once a day. Cheaper plans do not allow this, and a job that is never scheduled looks exactly like a job that is working.
steps: The three jobs are set in vercel.json: /api/cron/send-scheduled every 15 minutes, /api/cron/auto-search every 10 minutes, /api/cron/auto-tune daily at 13:00 UTC. Vercel's Hobby plan only allows daily runs, so the schedule needs the Pro plan.
Open the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Settings, Cron Jobs: all three paths listed with those schedules, and the team plan shows Pro (team Settings, Billing).
Prove they run: open the project's Logs tab, filter by path /api/cron/, and confirm entries roughly every 10 to 15 minutes over the last hour, with success statuses.
A job listed but with no log entries is exactly the silent failure this item warns about.

items.title: Plan allows long tasks
items.good: A single search can take several minutes because it chains many steps. On a smaller plan it is cut off part way and leaves work half done.
steps: The code asks for up to 300 seconds on the heavy routes (maxDuration = 300 in app/api/discover, app/api/draft, app/api/cron/auto-search, and app/api/cron/send-scheduled). Only the Vercel Pro plan honors that; Hobby cuts functions off far earlier.
Check the Vercel team plan says Pro (team Settings, Billing).
Prove it live: run a big real search on scout-source.com and confirm it keeps producing finds past the two-minute mark instead of dying near one minute.
A search that always stops around 60 seconds with an error in Vercel Logs means the plan is not honoring the duration.

items.title: Job failures get noticed
items.good: Right now a failing job is completely silent. That needs to change before launch.
steps: Today the only place a failed job shows is the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Logs tab, filtered by path /api/cron/ and level Error. Nothing emails anyone.
Minimum viable fix: name one person who opens that filtered view once a day during launch, and bookmark the exact filtered URL for them.
Better: have the technical partner add a Vercel log drain or a simple failure alert so errors push to email or Slack instead of waiting to be found.
Write down which of the two you chose and who owns it.

items.title: Watch each job run live
items.good: Not the code, the real scheduled run. It started, it did something, it finished.
steps: Open the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Logs, and filter by path /api/cron/.
send-scheduled (every 15 minutes): schedule one outreach email in Scout for a few minutes ahead, watch the log entry appear on the next tick, and confirm the email actually arrives.
auto-search (every 10 minutes): with an auto-search set up on your account, watch a run appear in the logs and confirm the digest email lands in your inbox.
auto-tune (daily 13:00 UTC, 8am Nashville): the morning after launch-eve, confirm its single daily entry ran without an error.
Pass per job: a log entry with a success status plus its real-world output (the email, the digest).

items.title: Leftover work gets picked up
items.good: Each run does as much as it safely can. The remainder should wait for the next run, not vanish.
steps: On a throwaway account, schedule a larger batch of sends (15 or more drafts) all for the same minute a few minutes ahead.
Watch the Vercel Logs (filter path /api/cron/send-scheduled) across two consecutive 15-minute ticks.

Pass: the first run sends part of the batch, the second run drains the rest, and the total number of emails that arrive equals the number scheduled. Anything scheduled that never sends and never errors is the fail this item exists to catch.
Use addresses you control as recipients so no stranger gets test mail.

sections.title: Taking money for real
sections.blurb: Everything here needs to be checked in live mode. Test mode proves nothing.

items.title: Payments live, not test
items.good: Live keys are in place and no test key is left anywhere in the live site.
steps: In the Stripe dashboard, switch the Test mode toggle off and confirm the products and recent activity you expect are visible in live mode.

Have the technical partner confirm the four Stripe values in Vercel (Settings, Environment Variables, Production) are live-mode: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY starts sk_live_, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET comes from the live-mode webhook endpoint, and STRIPE_PRICE_STARTER and STRIPE_PRICE_PRO are price IDs from live products. Any sk_test_ or test price ID is a fail.
Then prove it: subscribe on scout-source.com with a real card, confirm the charge appears in Stripe's live Payments, and refund yourself from the same screen.

items.title: Prices match the site
items.good: Fifteen dollars a month for thirty searches, thirty dollars for sixty, exactly as the pricing page says.
steps: Open the Stripe dashboard in live mode, Product catalog, and read the two subscription prices.

Compare against the pricing page on scout-source.com: Starter at 15 dollars a month for 30 searches, Pro at 30 dollars a month for 60 searches. Amount, currency, and monthly interval must match exactly.
Have the technical partner confirm the checkout uses those same two prices: the IDs shown in Stripe must equal STRIPE_PRICE_STARTER and STRIPE_PRICE_PRO in Vercel's Production environment variables.
Then click through checkout from the pricing page and confirm the amount on Stripe's payment screen matches what the page promised.

items.title: Webhooks reach the site
items.good: When someone pays, our site hears about it immediately and upgrades them. If this connection is wrong, people pay and nothing happens.
steps: Open the Stripe dashboard in live mode, Developers, Webhooks. There must be an endpoint for https://scout-source.com/api/billing/webhook listening to subscription and checkout events.
Click that endpoint and use Send test event. Pass: the attempt log shows a 200 response from our site. A 4xx or 5xx means paying customers would not get upgraded.
Also confirm the endpoint's signing secret is the same STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET stored in Vercel's Production environment variables (technical partner).
Final proof: make a real purchase and confirm the account flips to the paid plan inside Scout within a minute.

items.title: Refund position agreed
items.good: The rule is written down before the first request arrives, not decided during it.
steps: Agree it and put it on the terms page.

items.title: Payment inbox is read
items.good: Disputes and failed payments arrive by email and have a named owner.
steps: Stripe sends disputes and failed-payment notices to the account's email recipients: Stripe dashboard, Settings, then the Team and notification settings show exactly who gets them.
Read that recipient list and name the owner who acts on disputes (they have a deadline measured in days, not weeks).
Send yourself a test by triggering any notification and confirming it lands in the named inbox.

items.title: Sales tax decision made
items.good: Either we collect it, or we have deliberately decided we do not need to, based on where we are selling.
steps: Make the decision and record it.

sections.title: Locking Scout down
sections.blurb: Where security stands, in plain terms. The first group is already done and live, verify it rather than take our word. The second group is work only a human with the account passwords can do.

items.title: DONE: previews sandboxed
items.good: Websites shown inside Scout's preview used to be able to read your Scout login and act as you. They now run in a sealed frame with no access to anything of yours.
steps: Preview a few sites and confirm they still load and scroll normally.
That is the whole test; the protection is invisible when it works.
items.tech: Shipped. The technical change removed the previewed page's same-origin access.

items.title: DONE: endpoints gated
items.good: The features that cost us money per use (AI cleanup, website previews) refuse anyone who is not signed in, and have per-hour speed limits on top.
steps: Open a preview address in a private window: you get a sign-in page.
Confirmed live on the production site the day it shipped.

items.title: DONE: approve links expire
items.good: The approve buttons in digest emails stop working after two weeks, so a forwarded email is not a forever-key to sending from your account.
steps: Find a digest older than two weeks and click its approve link.
It should land on a clear link-expired message.

items.title: DONE: mailbox keys encrypted
items.good: The keys that let Scout send from connected Gmail and Outlook accounts are now encrypted in the database, so a database leak alone would yield gibberish.
steps: Each person who connected Gmail or Outlook before the change should disconnect and reconnect once, that re-saves their key in the scrambled form.

items.title: DONE: SSRF blocked
items.good: A classic attack makes an app fetch secret internal addresses by disguising them as normal links. Every disguise we know of is now blocked, and the blocks are covered by automated tests.
steps: Nothing to do by hand; noted here so the protection is on the record.

items.title: DONE: security headers on
items.good: The site now sends the standard protective headers, which stop other sites from framing Scout to trick clicks, among other classic tricks.
steps: Nothing to do by hand; verifiable with any online header checker against scout-source.com.

items.title: TO DO: two-factor the owners
items.good: Google, GitHub, Supabase, Vercel, and Stripe each need a second login step. One stolen password currently beats every protection above.
steps: Follow the separate Scout Lockdown checklist page, it walks each account step by step with time estimates.
About an hour total; this is the single most important open item.

items.title: TO DO: collaborators follow rules
items.good: Anyone with access (Delaney included) has two-factor on their accounts, their own login rather than a shared one, and access gets reviewed quarterly.
steps: Send collaborators the Scout Lockdown page.
List who has access to each of the five services and remove anyone who does not need it.

items.title: AT LAUNCH: real backups
items.good: The paid database plan turns on automatic daily backups, so a bad mistake is recoverable. Point-in-time recovery gets added once there are paying customers.
steps: This unlocks with the planned move to the Supabase Pro plan at launch.
After upgrading: Supabase dashboard, production project, Database, Backups. Pass: a daily schedule is shown and the first backup appears within a day.
Add point-in-time recovery on the same page once there are paying customers.
Put a reminder to check the page again one week after launch: a schedule that exists but has produced no backups is a fail.

items.title: AT LAUNCH: split the databases
items.good: Development currently uses the same database as the live site, so experiments touch real data. A separate practice copy ends that.
steps: The technical partner creates a second Supabase project (a dev copy), runs the same supabase/*.sql scripts into it, and points the laptop's ~/scout-web/.env.local at it.
Your verification: have the NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL from .env.local and the one in Vercel's Production environment variables shown side by side; they must contain different project identifiers.
Final proof: create a junk account while running the app locally and confirm it never appears in the production Supabase dashboard's Authentication user list.

items.title: LATER: dependency advisory
items.good: One low-risk security notice remains in a building block of the site; clearing it requires a major framework upgrade that deserves its own careful pass.
steps: Scheduled as deliberate post-launch work; automatic weekly dependency checks are already running in the meantime.

sections.title: Trust, privacy, and the law
sections.blurb: We store contact details for people who never signed up for anything. That deserves a deliberate position, decided by us, before someone asks.

items.title: Policy matches reality
items.good: Both pages are current, linked from the footer and from signup, and give a real address for questions.
steps: The pages are https://scout-source.com/privacy and https://scout-source.com/terms.

Read both against the real product: accounts, teams, payments via Stripe, email sending through connected Gmail and Outlook, automated searching, the shared index. Anything the product does that the policy does not mention gets flagged.
Check both are linked from the site footer and from the signup screen, and that the contact address printed in them is one a real person reads (send it a test email).
Pass: nothing in either page contradicts the product, and the test email gets answered.

items.title: Outside services disclosed
items.good: Profiles, uploaded files, and page content are sent to outside search and writing services. Users should learn that from our policy, not from someone else.
steps: Open https://scout-source.com/privacy and look for a section on third-party services.

It must plainly cover, at minimum: Anthropic (the AI that reads profiles, resumes, and pages, and writes drafts), Tavily (web search), Stripe (payments), Resend (email delivery), Google and Microsoft (connected mailboxes), and People Data Labs if enrichment is on.
Read the sentence aloud to someone outside the team; if they cannot say back roughly where their resume text goes, it is not plain enough.

items.title: Non-user data position set
items.good: We know how long we keep contact details, what a removal request looks like, and where someone sends one.
steps: Decide the three answers: how long contact details of non-users are kept, what someone must send to be removed, and which address takes the request.
Have them written into https://scout-source.com/privacy in their own short section.
Send a removal request to that address yourself from a personal account and confirm a human answers within the stated time.

items.title: Email law checked
items.good: Honest subject lines, a real identifiable sender, opt-outs honoured promptly, and any address disclosure that applies to us.
steps: Take two real messages: one outreach email sent through a connected mailbox, and one Scout digest email.
Check each against the CAN-SPAM basics: the subject line is honest about the content, the sender is identifiably you or Scout, and opting out is possible and honored promptly.
Click the unsubscribe link in a digest yourself and confirm the address actually stops receiving (the link is signed by the unsubscribe system, so it should work from the email without signing in).
Check whether the physical mailing address requirement applies to Scout's own marketing mail and decide what address to print; write the decision down.

items.title: Data requests possible
items.good: Reachable inside the product, with a named person responsible for answering within a stated time.
steps: On a throwaway account, look for Delete account where a stranger would look: the profile or settings area. Finding it only via a support email is a needs-work; not finding it at all is the fail (the endpoint exists at /api/account/delete, so the button should too).
Delete the throwaway account and confirm you can no longer sign in with it.
For data export: confirm the privacy page names an address for asking for your data, and that a named person owns answering within the stated time.

items.title: Support inbox is read
items.good: One address, one named owner, and a stated response time.
steps: Pick the address, name its owner, and agree a response time you would put in writing.
Publish it in the site footer and on the terms and privacy pages.
Test: send a question to it from an outside account and confirm the owner answers within the stated time without being nudged.

sections.title: The live site and knowing when it breaks
sections.blurb: How people find us, and how we hear about problems before customers tell us.

items.title: www and bare domain work
items.good: Both forms load over a secure connection, and one redirects to the other rather than both being separately live.
steps: Try both in a browser and watch the address bar.

items.title: Breakage gets noticed
items.good: Errors on the live site raise an alert to a person. Without this, the first sign of trouble is a customer telling us, if they bother.
steps: Know the honest starting point: nothing in the code sends error alerts today. Errors only appear in the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Logs tab, when someone looks.

Decide the launch answer: either the technical partner wires an alerting service (Sentry, or a Vercel log drain that emails on errors), or a named person checks the Logs tab filtered to Error at agreed times each day.
Whichever you pick, test it: break something harmless on purpose (a bad request to a real endpoint), and confirm the error either raises an alert or is spotted in the next scheduled log check.
Do not mark this done on the phrase 'we would see it'; the test is that somebody actually saw it.

items.title: Uptime is watched
items.good: A regular automatic check on both the public page and one signed-in feature, because the front page can look perfectly fine while everything behind sign-in is down.
steps: Use a free uptime service (UptimeRobot or similar): add a monitor for https://scout-source.com checking every 5 minutes.
Add a second monitor for https://scout-source.com/api/build-id, which exercises the server side rather than just the front page.
Point alerts at a phone (the app's push notification or SMS), not just email, and confirm by pausing a monitor or watching a real alert fire once.
A true signed-in synthetic check is a later nice-to-have; these two monitors are the launch bar.

items.title: Old site redirects
items.good: The retired address redirects to the real one, so there are not two live copies of the product.
steps: The old address is https://cue-connect-alpha.vercel.app (the redirect is wired in middleware.ts).
Open it in a browser and watch the address bar: it must land on https://scout-source.com without you touching anything.
Also try a deep link like https://cue-connect-alpha.vercel.app/app and confirm it redirects too, signed in or out.

items.title: Shared links look right
items.good: Pasting the site into a message shows a proper title, description, and image.
steps: Paste the link into a chat and look at the preview.

items.title: Visitors are counted
items.good: Not just installed. Load the site and watch the visit appear.
steps: Open the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Analytics tab. If it offers an Enable button, nothing is being recorded yet: enabling needs the technical partner to add Vercel's analytics package and redeploy.
Once enabled, open scout-source.com in a private window, then watch the Analytics tab show the visit within a minute or two.
Pass is the watched visit appearing, not the tool being installed.

items.title: Search engines directed
items.good: The public pages can be found, and everything behind sign-in is excluded.
steps: Open https://scout-source.com/robots.txt in a browser. Pass: it allows the public site and disallows /app, /admin, /api/, /auto/, and /readiness (this is generated from app/robots.ts).
Open https://scout-source.com/sitemap.xml and confirm it lists the public pages (generated from app/sitemap.ts).
If either address 404s on the live site, the code has not been deployed; redeploy and check again.
Optional later: submit the sitemap in Google Search Console so indexing starts sooner.

items.title: A status page exists
items.good: Even a pinned post. People forgive outages, they do not forgive silence.
steps: Decide where it lives.

sections.title: Launch day, in order
sections.blurb: The one place where the order genuinely matters. Do these top to bottom.

items.title: 1. Freeze and confirm the build
items.good: No further changes except fixes for things on this page.
steps: Announce the freeze so everyone knows.

items.title: 2. Back up, run setup scripts
items.good: Backup first, every time, even for a script that says it is safe to re-run.
steps: Backup: Supabase dashboard, production project, Database, Backups shows one from today (paid plan), or the technical partner takes a manual export and shows you the file.

Run: Supabase SQL Editor, paste and run supabase/RUN-ME-catchup.sql, then supabase/RUN-ME-missing-tables.sql, then any per-feature .sql file not yet ticked off on the database section's list. All are safe to re-run.
Confirm: run the table-list query from the database section and tick each expected table, then do one in-app proof (save a company location, run one search, star one find).

items.title: 3. Live settings, republish
items.good: Settings do not take effect until the site is published again. Republishing is part of setting them.
steps: Set: Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Settings, Environment Variables, Production; work through the full checklist from the Keys and settings section.
Publish: Deployments tab, latest Production deployment, three-dot menu, Redeploy. Nothing takes effect before this.
Spot-check one setting-dependent feature end to end: sign in with Google (proves the site address settings) and load a website preview (proves the signing secrets).

items.title: 4. Payments live, prove webhook
items.good: A test notification from the payment dashboard is accepted by our site before any real customer tries it.
steps: Stripe dashboard in live mode, Developers, Webhooks, open the https://scout-source.com/api/billing/webhook endpoint, click Send test event.
Pass: the endpoint's attempt log shows a 200 response.
Then the real proof: buy a plan on scout-source.com with a real card, watch the account upgrade inside Scout within a minute, and refund the charge from Stripe's Payments screen.

items.title: 5. Smoke-test part one live
items.good: Sign up, search, draft, send, and buy. Fresh account, real card, real inbox.
steps: If any step needs a workaround, we are not launched yet.

items.title: 6. Jobs on last, watch each
items.good: Turn them on only once the data they act on is known to be good.
steps: Know the mechanics: the three jobs ship with the deploy (they are declared in vercel.json), so 'turning them on last' means making the launch deploy after the data and settings work is done, not flipping a switch.

After the launch deploy, open the Vercel dashboard, scout-web project, Logs, filter path /api/cron/, and stay until you have seen each of the three paths run once: send-scheduled within 15 minutes, auto-search within 10, auto-tune at its daily 13:00 UTC slot.
For each, confirm the real-world output described in the scheduled-jobs section (the sent email, the digest) before walking away.

items.title: 7. Announce, watch two days
items.good: Agreed in advance: who is watching, when, and what would make us roll back.
steps: Put names against the hours.

items.title: 8. Write down what broke
items.good: While it is still fresh. It becomes the next version of this page.
steps: Book the half hour now.

glossary: Publishing, or deploying
Putting the newest version of the code onto the live website. Until it is published, a finished change only exists on a developer's computer.
Rolling back
Putting the live website back to the previous version, usually within a couple of minutes. This is our undo button.
A setting, or environment variable
A value stored outside the code, like a password or a web address. They are set separately for the test site and the live site, and only take effect the next time the site is published.
A key
A long password that lets our site use somebody else's service, such as the writing or search services. Anyone who has the key can spend our money with it.
A setup script, or migration
A one-off instruction that adds new tables to the database so a feature has somewhere to store things. If it has not been run, the feature quietly does nothing.
A background job, or cron
Something the site does on a timer with nobody watching, such as sending scheduled messages every fifteen minutes.
A rate limit
A cap on how many times something can be used in a period, so one person cannot run up an enormous bill or overload the site.
The live site versus the test site
The live site is what customers use. The test site is a copy for trying things. They have separate settings and should have separate databases.
Signing in with Google or Microsoft
Letting Scout act on your mailbox without ever knowing your password. The permission can be withdrawn at any time from your own account settings.
A webhook
One service telling another that something happened, for example the payment service telling Scout that someone just paid.
Two-factor authentication
A second step at login (a code or fingerprint) so a stolen password alone is not enough to get in.
Encrypted at rest
Stored in scrambled form, so someone who steals the database file still cannot read the sensitive values.
Expiring link
A link that stops working after a set time, so an old forwarded email cannot be used as a permanent key.
